catalogTitle: The Lesson of the בני מכיר and the בנות צלפחד: Our Eternal Connection to Eretz Yisroel

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every Jew, like every shidduch, is drawn back to his origin in Eretz Yisrael, and that the Bnei Machir and the daughters of Tzelafchad, the family that held Gilad, carry the law of return that Eliyahu will announce at the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Moshe, in Sefer Devarim, retells that he gave Gilad to Machir, something the people saw only months before. He links three episodes about the family of Machir: their conquest of Gilad, the daughters of Tzelafchad's request for a nachalah, and the complaint of the Bnei Machir that ends Bamidbar. The daughters waited forty years for a fitting match and are praised, while Nadav and Avihu are criticized for the same; the Rav explains through the principle that everything is drawn to its origin: the isha to the ish, Adam to the earth of the mizbeach and Eretz Yisrael. Once the daughters received a nachalah they were joined to their root and found their shidduch at once. Gilad, the land of Eliyahu HaGiladi, is the place of Yovel, the law of return, which only Rachel's children could conquer. He ends that Shabbos Chazon is a Shabbos of hope and a great eis ratzon.

en: Everything is drawn back to its origin: the isha to the ish she came from, and Adam to the earth of the mizbeach from which he was formed.
The Rav explains that a person with a pure heart can rely on the inclination of his heart in choosing a shidduch, because it draws him to his true match.
The daughters of Tzelafchad found their shidduch only after they received a nachalah, because that joined them to Eretz Yisrael, the root of their root.
Yovel is the law of return, and Eliyahu HaNavi, who lived in Gilad, is the one who will announce the great return of Klal Yisrael.
Gilad, the land of return, could be conquered only by Rachel's children, which is why Moshe left it for the Bnei Machir of Menashe.
Shabbos Chazon is not only a Shabbos of sorrow; the Rav calls it a Shabbos of hope, when the heart can see the third Beis HaMikdash, and a great eis ratzon.

title.en: Why Moshe retells recent events

summary.en: The Rav opens with Moshe's recounting to the new generation at the start of Sefer Devarim, and asks what purpose there is in telling them about the war with Sichon and Og and the giving of Gilad, events that happened only five or six months earlier.

title.en: The complaint of the Bnei Machir

summary.en: The Rav describes the complaint at the end of Bamidbar: the family of Machir feared that the daughters of Tzelafchad would marry into another shevet and their nachalah would pass out of Menashe, and Moshe tells them they are right. He notes this is the third episode involving this family, after Gilad and the daughters' own request for a nachalah.

title.en: Waiting forty years: praised or criticized?

summary.en: The Rav ties the three episodes together and brings the Midrash that the daughters of Tzelafchad waited forty years for a fitting match and are praised for it. He contrasts this with Chazal's criticism of Nadav and Avihu for not marrying because no one was good enough, and asks how the two fit together.

title.en: The match under their nose; the heart decides

summary.en: The Rav points out that the daughters finally married their own cousins, who lived nearby all along, and insists nothing happens by chance. He brings a letter answering someone torn between two shidduchim: no one today can decide for him, but Hashem guides through the inclination of the heart.

title.en: Everything is drawn to its origin

summary.en: The Rav asks why the heart should decide a shidduch and answers with the law that everything is drawn to its origin, contrasting the Torah's view with Newton's gravity. The isha comes from the ish, and Adam from the earth of the mizbeach, so a match is a reunion; this explains the Gemara that the mizbeach weeps over one who divorces his first wife, and why one should follow a pure heart.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, the root of the root

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew belongs to Eretz Yisrael and must return there, and that one cut off from his wife is cut off from Eretz Yisrael too, as hinted in the first Mishnah of Gittin. The daughters of Tzelafchad, as tzidkaniyos, relied on their heart, which drew them to no one until their nachalah tied them to Eretz Yisrael; then their shidduch appeared. The parsha read before Chodesh Av repairs the sin of the meraglim, who did not long for the eretz chemdah.

title.en: Why Moshe did not take Gilad

summary.en: The Rav returns to the Bnei Machir, who went to Gilad and drove out the Emori there. He explains that Amon and Moav were off-limits, and Moshe could take their former land only because Sichon had conquered it, and asks why Moshe stopped short of Gilad and left it for the Bnei Machir.

title.en: Kiryas Sefer and the forgotten halachos

summary.en: The Rav brings Kalev's promise to whoever would conquer Kiryas Sefer, and the Gemara in Temurah that Osniel ben Kenaz restored the three thousand halachos forgotten in the days of mourning for Moshe. He cites an explanation that the Torah is written into the land of Eretz Yisrael, so that conquering a piece of land gave Osniel a connection to the halachos hidden in it.

title.en: Gilad and Yovel, the law of return

summary.en: The Rav proposes that Gilad is connected to the parsha of Yovel, the law of return. Land in Eretz Yisrael that is bought returns to its owner, because it belongs to his neshamah; the eved who took a shifchah that is not his goes free at Yovel. Every Jew, wherever he is, will return to Yerushalayim and the place of the mizbeach, and he cites the Arizal that even very sinful souls will eventually return.

title.en: Eliyahu HaGiladi, herald of the return

summary.en: The Rav explains that Eliyahu HaNavi is the herald of Yovel who will return children to parents and Klal Yisrael to Hashem and to Eretz Yisrael, and that Yovel and teshuvah are one. Eliyahu chose to live in Gilad, the land of Yovel, and brought the people back to Hashem at Har HaCarmel. He then asks why Moshe did not fight Amalek himself.

title.en: Rachel's children, Amalek and Gilad

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that only Rachel's children can overcome Amalek, so Moshe, from Levi, sent Yehoshua. Purim will not be nullified because Amalek was never fully erased; that will come with Mashiach. Rachel is the neshamah of return, as the navi promises her that her children will return, and therefore only her children, Menashe's family of Machir, could conquer Gilad, the land of return that Moshe left over.

title.en: Shabbos Chazon: a Shabbos of hope

summary.en: The Rav teaches that Shabbos Chazon is not what it seems on the surface: beyond the sorrow, it is the Shabbos before what Tisha B'Av is meant to become, the greatest moed. He brings that on Shabbos Chazon Hashem shows each Jew the third Beis HaMikdash, each according to how much he felt the mourning for Yerushalayim, and that the heart can see.

title.en: Sefer Devarim: Torah for the seventy exiles

summary.en: The Rav explains that Sefer Devarim, begun on this Shabbos, is a book of return rather than separation. He asks why Moshe explained the Torah in seventy languages a month before his passing, and, through the wagons Yosef sent, connects the number seventy to galus. Moshe prepared the people for the seventieth, lowest level of galus by bringing the Torah down into every language, so that it would go down with them as a comfort.

title.en: Machir and Gilad: the answer

summary.en: The Rav answers his opening question: Moshe retold that he gave Gilad to Machir as a comfort, because Machir and Gilad stand for return and redemption at the end of galus, where Eliyahu HaGiladi will emerge. This is why only the Bnei Machir complained that a nachalah must not leave its shevet, and why the daughters of Tzelafchad married into Machir and received Gilad.

title.en: The great eis ratzon of Shabbos Chazon

summary.en: The Rav explains why Shabbos afternoon is a great eis ratzon even though the afternoon is otherwise a time of din, and says that Shabbos Chazon, amid the days of din, is entirely one great eis ratzon. He urges using every moment of it and closes with a brachah that Tisha B'Av turn to joy.

catalogTitle: ב) בנר חנוכה משלימים כתר של משיח

oneLiner.en: Building on a Sfas Emes, the Rav explains that Chanukah, a miracle of the eighth that stands above nature and calculation, kindles the hidden spark of Yiddishkeit and the light of Moshiach that is in every Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav reads a Sfas Emes: on Chanukah, when blessing rests on the little, every Jew must strengthen himself in the one point of Yiddishkeit within him. To explain it he brings the Maharal: seven is the number of nature, eight is above nature and calculation, which is why milah is on the eighth day and why Torah belongs to the eighth. The Chanukah miracles, oil that burned eight times its measure and the few who beat the many, were miracles of the eighth. So its essence is Zos Chanukah, when one day holds more than a day, like Yovel, Eretz Yisrael and the Beis Hamikdash. Every Jew's spark from Avraham Avinu cannot be extinguished, and Chanukah lights reveal his hidden light, as a story of the Chozeh of Lublin shows. He closes with Zos Chanukah as a day of good resolutions.

en: According to the Sfas Emes, on Chanukah every Jew must strengthen himself in the single point of Yiddishkeit found in him, however small he thinks it is.
Citing the Maharal, the Rav explains that seven stands for the natural world created in seven days, while eight is above nature and above calculation; therefore milah is on the eighth day.
The Chanukah miracles were miracles of the eighth: the oil burned eight times its natural measure, and the few defeated the many without regard to calculation.
The essence of Chanukah is its eighth day, Zos Chanukah, which is not limited to what one day can hold, like the fiftieth year of Yovel.
Every Jew carries a spark inherited from Avraham Avinu that can never be extinguished, and on Chanukah Hashem takes up its cause against the forces that cover it.
Chanukah lights reveal the hidden light within each Jew, how he will look in the days of Moshiach.

title.en: The Sfas Emes and the Maharal on seven and eight

summary.en: The Rav reads the Sfas Emes that on Chanukah every Jew must strengthen himself in his one point of Yiddishkeit. He begins to explain it with the Maharal: seven is the number of nature, eight is above it, which is why milah, cutting off what nature put there, is on the eighth day.

title.en: The Chanukah miracles as miracles of the eighth

summary.en: The Rav explains that Torah is above nature and belongs to the eighth, and that the oil burning eight times its measure and the few defeating the many were miracles above calculation. In a world of mostly evil and little good, the little prevailed; therefore Chanukah is eight days and its essence is the eighth day, Zos Chanukah.

title.en: Zos Chanukah: a little that holds a lot

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the daily reading of one nasi with Zos Chanukah, which holds more than one day, and the custom of burning all the leftover wicks together. He compares it to Yovel, Eretz Yisrael and the Beis Hamikdash, places above measure, and through the Maharal on Tehillim 19 ties the eighth to Torah, whose victory over the Greeks is Chanukah.

title.en: The unquenchable spark and the hidden light

summary.en: Returning to the Sfas Emes, the Rav explains that every Jew has a spark from Avraham Avinu that can never be extinguished, burning openly in tzaddikim and hidden in others. On Chanukah Hashem avenges its covering, and the Chanukah lights, which hold the hidden light of creation, can kindle the hidden light within each Jew.

title.en: The Chozeh's kvittel and the resolutions of Zos Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav tells a story the Chiddushei HaRim told: the Chozeh of Lublin would not act against an informer because, on the night of the first kvittel, the man's Chanukah lights were shining in all worlds; Chanukah lights reveal a Jew's hidden light, the light of Moshiach. He closes by calling the eighth day a day of good resolutions and blesses all Jews with a great yeshuah.

catalogTitle: ע"י נר חנוכה זוכים לראות אור הגנוז בתורה כל השנה

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that the hidden light of creation, the Ohr HaGanuz, rests in the Chanukah lights and in every Jew, and that the Greek war against Jewish havdalah and kedushah is answered by Chanukah's light.

abstract.en: The Rav teaches that the Ohr HaGanuz, the light of creation that Hashem hid away, is concealed in the Chanukah lights and in the Torah, and that through the Chanukah lights one can glimpse it in learning. That light served for thirty-six hours, and the Chanukah lights add up to thirty-six. He then presents the Greek war as a war on havdalah: their decrees against Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah and their breaches in the fence of the Beis HaMikdash came from refusing to accept that Israel is set apart. Havdalah is a foundation of creation, as Korach's end shows, and light belongs to kedushah while night is the time of darkness. The Greeks glorified the body and pushed into the place of kedushah, while Chanukah carries kedushah outward. Finally, every Jew keeps a sealed jug of oil, a hidden light that Chanukah can bring out.

en: The Ohr HaGanuz, hidden since creation, is hidden in the Chanukah lights, and through them one can see it in the Torah.
The hidden light served for thirty-six hours, and the Chanukah lights over eight nights add up to thirty-six.
The Greeks fought the havdalah between Israel and the nations: they decreed against Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah and broke breaches in the fence of the Beis HaMikdash.
Havdalah is a foundation of creation, and Korach, who wanted to undo the havdalah of Aharon, was swallowed into the earth.
The Greeks made the body and its strength into an end in itself, and Chanukah is the yom tov of the soul against the body.
Every Jew keeps a point of Yiddishkeit that cannot be extinguished, a hidden light that shines when he does teshuvah.

title.en: The Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh

summary.en: In a badly garbled opening, the Rav speaks of how precious Chanukah is and says that it was established for the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh for Torah and mitzvos, not only for the victory.

title.en: The hidden light in the Chanukah lights

summary.en: The Rav explains that the first light of creation was hidden away, in the Torah and in the Chanukah lights, so that simple Jews looking at the lights see something of it. That light served thirty-six hours, and the Chanukah lights add up to thirty-six.

title.en: New lights in learning Gemara

summary.en: The Rav says that one who connects himself to the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh can see, between the letters of a Gemara, new lights, just as each night of Chanukah adds a new light.

title.en: Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Greeks decreed against Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah because these show the kedushah of Israel: the Greeks held that Jews are no different from other nations, while Shabbos was given to Israel alone and havdalah separates Israel from the nations like light from darkness.

title.en: Breaches in the fence of the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Rav brings a Midrash that the nations resent the Jews' extra mitzvos, and notes that Chanukah was the last mitzvah given. He describes the fence around the Beis HaMikdash beyond which a non-Jew could not pass, and explains that the Greeks broke breaches in it because they refused to accept the havdalah between Israel and the nations.

title.en: Havdalah as a foundation of creation

summary.en: The Rav shows from Bereishis that havdalah is part of creation, and brings Korach, who wanted to abolish the havdalah of Aharon and was answered that Hashem set boundaries like morning and night; he was swallowed into the earth. Hashem gave the light to kedushah, which is why nearly all mitzvos are done by day.

title.en: The darkness of night and winter

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Hashem does not attach His name to darkness, and the passuk that at night the beasts of the forest come out. Night is harder for the sick and more dangerous, and the long winter nights around Chanukah are the time of greatest darkness.

title.en: Yavan pushes into kedushah; Chanukah goes outward

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the private domain of the Ribono shel Olam with the public domain, and explains that the Greeks wanted to break the walls and bring darkness into the place of kedushah, as the letters of Yavan, a yud stretched into a vav and a nun, show. On Chanukah, Jews go the other way, carrying kedushah out into the public domain with more light each night.

title.en: The body: elevated or glorified

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew gives Hashem a share even in eating, sleeping and caring for his health, serving Him with both inclinations. The Greeks instead made the body and sport an end in themselves, and built a place for games beside the Beis HaMikdash; Chanukah is the yom tov against the body.

title.en: The sealed jug of oil in every Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Greeks wanted the Torah forgotten, but Jews have a promise that it will never be forgotten; the Greeks ruled the Beis HaMikdash but not the sealed jug of oil. So too every Jew is a whole world with his own Beis HaMikdash, and even if it is breached a point of Yiddishkeit remains that shines when he does teshuvah.

title.en: The soul as a lamp; Shabbos Chanukah

summary.en: In a garbled stretch the Rav compares a Jewish soul to a lamp of wick, oil and flame, and contrasts the Shabbos lights with the Chanukah lights, which reveal the hidden light. He adds that what a person could not reach before can be grasped on Chanukah, on Shabbos Chanukah and on Zos Chanukah.

title.en: The ox's horn and the hidden strengths of the soul

summary.en: The Rav explains the Greek decree to write on the horn of the ox that Jews have no share in the G-d of Israel, and says Chanukah is the soul's victory over the body. When the yetzer hara claims that all of a person's 'oils', his thoughts, are defiled, a sealed jug remains; a person has hidden strengths, and Chanukah is the time to bring out the hidden light of the soul.

catalogTitle: דרוש בנס חנוכה - נס הנרות מגלים נס המלחמה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah victory was a miracle wrought through the power of Torah, which cannot openly break nature, and that the miracle of the oil in the Beis HaMikdash revealed that the war itself was a miracle.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Al HaNissim speaks only of the war and not of the oil, and what 'the wicked into the hands of those who toil in Your Torah' adds. He turns to the Gemara in Megillah: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads 'bayis gadol' as a place where Torah is magnified, Rabbi Yochanan as a place where tefillah is magnified, since Elisha did his wonders through prayer. He brings the Chasam Sofer, who asks why Elisha could not have used holy Names, and answers from the Yerushalmi. The Rav adds a third power, Torah, and explains that Torah cannot make miracles outside nature, because nature itself follows the Torah, except in the place of the Mikdash, where heaven meets earth. The Chashmonaim's victory came through Torah and looked natural; the oil, a miracle of the same kind, revealed it. He closes with the chanukas habayis of the beis medrash and a tefillah for the Shechinah to rest there.

en: Al HaNissim and HaNeiros Hallalu speak of the victory in the war and not of the oil burning eight days.
The dispute over 'bayis gadol' is not about whether Torah or tefillah is greater, but whether a place adds more to tefillah or to Torah.
Miracles can be made through tefillah, through holy Names, and also through the power of Torah, which stands on a higher level.
Through Torah one cannot make a miracle outside nature, because nature itself runs by the Torah's laws, except in the place of the Mikdash, where heaven and earth meet.
The Chashmonaim's victory came through the power of Torah, and the miracle of the oil, of the same measure, showed that the war too was a miracle.
The true building of a beis medrash is the Jews who come there to learn and daven.

title.en: Why Al HaNissim mentions only the war

summary.en: The Rav notes that Al HaNissim and HaNeiros Hallalu speak only of the victory, not of the oil, and brings the views on which miracle Chanukah celebrates. He then asks what 'the wicked into the hands of those who toil in Your Torah' adds after 'the wicked into the hands of the righteous'.

title.en: Beis haknesses, beis medrash and 'bayis gadol'

summary.en: The Rav learns the Gemara in Megillah on turning a shul into a beis medrash, and the dispute whether 'bayis gadol' means a place where Torah or tefillah is magnified. He explains that the dispute is which kind of place adds more: a shul to tefillah, or a beis medrash to Torah.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: Elisha, tefillah or holy Names

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's question: how does Rabbi Yochanan know that Elisha did his wonders through prayer and not through holy Names? He answers from the Yerushalmi that one who benefits from others may not use the Names, while the Bavli does not hold so; the Rav says he finds it hard to say that Elisha worked with Names.

title.en: The power of Torah and the laws of nature

summary.en: The Rav adds a third power for miracles, Torah, and asks why Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi did not answer that Elisha worked through Torah. He explains that Torah created the world and nature follows its laws, so Torah does not change nature; a tzaddik who wants a miracle beyond nature must daven.

title.en: The Mikdash, where heaven meets earth

summary.en: The Rav explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's miracles were set as a condition at Creation, and that the place of the Mikdash, where heaven ends and earth begins, runs by heavenly rules beyond reckoning. He brings the ner hamaaravi that burned beyond its measure of oil as such a miracle dictated by the Torah.

title.en: The oil revealed the miracle of the war

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Chashmonaim, who gave their lives for Torah, won through the power of Torah, so their victory looked natural. Hashem made the oil, a miracle of 'the few holding the many' like 'the many into the hands of the few', in the Mikdash to show the war was a miracle; this answers why Al HaNissim speaks of the war.

title.en: Chanukas habayis of the beis medrash

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the dedication of the beis medrash on this day, a place magnified in both Torah and tefillah whose walls are soaked with them. He says the true building is the Jews who come to learn and daven, 'Heichal Hashem', and asks Hashem, with Moshe's prayer 'vihi noam', that the Shechinah rest there.

catalogTitle: “נשלחה אנשים לפנינו” - The Importance of Being a שליח of 'ה

oneLiner.en: Starting from the two accounts of who sent the meraglim, the Rav teaches that every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem with a personal mission hidden in his name, and that in the days of Tammuz and Av, and in the end of days, he must hold on to emunah and remember whose shaliach he is.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Parshas Devarim says the people asked to send spies while Parshas Shelach says Hashem commanded it. He brings the Chasam Sofer: the power of the sender rests in the agent, and the people's bad intentions spoiled the mission. The Rav reverses it: the people asked first, and Hashem joined as a sender so the meraglim would at least have a choice, which saved Kalev and Yehoshua. From here he explains that every Jew doing a mitzvah is Hashem's shaliach; each has a unique mission carried in his name, and the yetzer hara's own mission is to make him forget it. Tammuz and Av are the days of the Samech-Mem's power, but under the deepest tumah lies the greatest kedusha. The meraglim's sin was going by reason instead of emunah. Tzitzis, at the bottom of the garment, is the reminder for the end of days. He closes with Hashem's love for every Jew and the vision of the third Beis HaMikdash on Shabbos Chazon.

en: Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that the power and intention of the sender pass into the agent, so the people's flawed intention harmed the meraglim, just as a congregation's intentions affect its shliach tzibbur.
Every Jew who does a mitzvah because Hashem commanded it is Hashem's shaliach and carries His power.
Each person comes into the world with a unique mission that is carried in his name, and the yetzer hara's own mission is to make him forget it.
Tammuz and Av are days when the Samech-Mem has special power, and correcting the sin of the meraglim means holding on to emunah in these days.
The greater the kedusha, the more it is covered with tumah, so the days of Bein HaMetzarim hide the greatest potential for closeness to Hashem.
Tzitzis is the remedy for the end of days: it reminds a Jew whose shaliach he is.
Hashem loves every Jew, even the worst, and one must not let the Satan persuade him otherwise.

title.en: Who sent the meraglim: the Chasam Sofer

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Devarim, where the people ask to send spies, with Shelach, where Hashem says 'send for yourself men'. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the sender's power rests in the agent, so the people's flawed intention spoiled the mission, as with a shliach tzibbur.

title.en: Why Devarim may open with rebuke

summary.en: In a side point, the Rav brings Rashi that Bamidbar does not open with Pesach Sheini because a sefer should not open with Klal Yisrael's disgrace, and asks why Devarim opens with rebuke. He answers that Devarim is Moshe's own words, and having a leader who rebukes them is itself their praise.

title.en: Hashem joins as sender to give a choice

summary.en: The Rav offers two readings: Hashem took the blame on Himself in Shelach, or, as the Rav prefers, the people asked first and Hashem added Himself as a sender so His intention would count too. This gave the meraglim a choice and saved Kalev and Yehoshua.

title.en: Every Jew is Hashem's shaliach

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew who does a mitzvah is Hashem's shaliach and carries His power, illustrated by the scribe who may not sit on one bench with the Sefer Torah he wrote. When a Jew forgets his mission, Hashem sends him thoughts of teshuvah, which a busy person brushes off.

title.en: Whose shaliach are you? The source of shlichus

summary.en: Picturing people rushing along a New York avenue, the Rav asks whose shaliach each one is: Hashem's or his yetzer's. He explains that shlichus needs a neshama that is a part of G-d, that it was first given with the korban Pesach when the Jews became a people, and that Moshe wanted the meraglim to carry this G-dly power of shlichus.

title.en: A person's mission is in his name

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shelah's practice of saying a passuk for one's name at the end of Shemoneh Esrei, and explains that each Jew has a unique mission carried in his name, citing Rashi that angels' names change with their mission and the Arizal on a father's naming. Leaving Shemoneh Esrei for the marketplace, one easily forgets his mission, and the passuk reminds him.

title.en: The angel's answer and the names in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav asks why the angel answered Yaakov's 'tell me your name' with 'why do you ask my name', and explains that this was his true answer: the mission of the Satan is to make a person not ask his own name. Likewise the Torah repeats the names of Bnei Yisrael going down to Mitzrayim, in Vayigash and again in Shemos, so they would not forget their mission there.

title.en: The meraglim's names and the days of bikurei anavim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah repeats the meraglim's names to remind them they were Moshe's shluchim, not agents of their own interests, which the Zohar describes. Their mission fell in Tammuz and Av, the season of the Samech-Mem's power, hinted in 'yemei bikurei anavim': the letters before those of 'anavim' spell the Satan's name.

title.en: Amalek in the Negev: reason against emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains 'Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev' as the power of the Samech-Mem in these dry days, and that the three weeks and nine days exist to correct the sin of the meraglim. He says the meraglim were right by reason that they could not conquer the land; their sin was going with reason instead of with emunah.

title.en: Hidden kedusha and Mashiach in Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Rav teaches that the higher the kedusha, the more it is covered by tumah, so in Bein HaMetzarim one can reach more than at any other time, and these days will be the greatest festivals when Mashiach comes. Mashiach is hidden in them, born on Tisha B'Av, and Tammuz and Menachem Av are in gematria 'Melech HaMashiach'. Shelach ends with tzitzis as the reminder of one's mission.

title.en: Acharis hayamim and the tzitzis at the edge

summary.en: Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Rav calls the three weeks the 'end of the days' of the year, matching the end of days in history, the heels of Mashiach, when Jews have fallen lower than ever, kept afloat only by Torah. Tzitzis, which reminded the student in the Gemara Menachos who he was, hang at the bottom of the garment, and Moshe saw his people struggling to swim to the shore of Mashiach.

title.en: Weaving the garment of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that each person weaves a garment of 613 threads with his mitzvos, and Klal Yisrael weaves a collective garment since Matan Torah; this generation weaves the last thread, where Mashiach is found. He adds that Krias Shema's last word 'emes' is not written and must be added with force, as emes is hidden in the end of days.

title.en: Vacation, the garment, and daily mussar

summary.en: The Rav describes the summer pull of Tammuz and Av, when people on vacation first take off their garments, and recalls that after Adam's sin Hashem gave him garments as protection. Since even the meraglim forgot, he says one needs reminders, and advises learning some mussar every day.

title.en: Hashem loves every Jew

summary.en: The Rav says the Satan tells a person that Hashem hates him, as the meraglim's generation claimed, and Rashi answers that Hashem loves them. He tells of a chassid who traveled days just to see his Rebbe, who told him his love for his chassidim is nothing compared to Hashem's love for even a moser. He stresses that love is a need like food, for children and even malachim, and that Tisha B'Av's readings open with 'banim'.

title.en: Malachi's message and Shabbos Chazon

summary.en: The Rav explains that Malachi, the last navi, left a message for the whole exile until Eliyahu comes. He then speaks of Shabbos Chazon, when one can see the third Beis HaMikdash, brings gematrios on Parshas Devarim and Tehillim 89, urges preparing well for this Shabbos, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: מדליקין הנרות עד שאפילו הנפשות הנמוכות יאירו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah light, placed below ten tefachim and spreading outward night after night, is the Shechinah coming down to Jews in exile, and that each Jew, above all in his years of learning, must take in enough of its light to carry Torah into his whole life.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with ner ish u'veiso: beyond the miracle of the whole nation, each Jew should feel that a light burns for him personally. Yosef's two dreams show the same move, from Yosef watching from outside to the whole holy structure coming down to him in Egypt. The Chanukah light is placed below ten tefachim, although the Shechinah never descended below ten, because Chanukah is a festival of exile, a kind of bikur cholim in which Hashem comes down to the sick. Through the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel on the havdalah fire, the blue and white parts of a flame, and din and rachamim, he explains why the lights increase: one begins with aseh tov. He applies this to the years of yeshiva, criticizes young Jews who give themselves for foreign causes, reads the end of Niddah, and closes with Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, who saw his whole life as a free gift and a miracle.

en: The mitzvah of ner ish u'veiso teaches that each Jew should feel the Chanukah miracle as something happening to him personally, not only to the nation.
The Chanukah light is placed below ten tefachim because Chanukah is a festival of exile, when the Shechinah comes down to the Jews as one visits the sick.
Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel reflect din and rachamim, the consuming blue and the illuminating white of a flame; the halachah follows Beis Hillel because the world now runs with rachamim.
The lights increase each night because, per Beis Hillel, one starts with aseh tov and the sur mera follows on its own.
The years of yeshiva are the time of chinuch, when a bochur must fill himself with enough Torah to light his way for the rest of his life.
Like Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, a Jew who knows that everything he has is a free gift sees his whole life as a chain of miracles.

candidateTopics: Chanukah as a festival of exile

title.en: A light that burns for each Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah light testifies to the miracles of the whole nation, but a distant person is barely moved by a national event. The mitzvah of ner ish u'veiso asks each Jew to feel that a light burns for him personally and that the same miracles happen in his own life.

title.en: Yosef's two dreams

summary.en: Chanukah falls in the weeks of Yosef's dreams. In the first dream Yosef only watches the sheaves from outside; in the second the sun, moon and stars bow to him, and the Rav explains that the whole holy structure must come down to Yosef in exile in Egypt so that he does not sink there.

title.en: Below ten tefachim: the Shechinah visits the sick

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Chanukah light is placed below ten tefachim when the Shechinah never descended below ten, and answers that Chanukah is a festival of exile, when the Jews are sick, and at bikur cholim the great go down to the small, as with Chizkiyahu and Yeshayahu. He adds that the light of Chanukah must not only be received but lit onward to others.

title.en: Me'or or me'orei: the colors of a flame

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah where Beis Shammai say 'shebara me'or ha'esh' and Beis Hillel 'borei me'orei ha'esh', and describes the flame: a white part above that gives light, and a blue part around the wick that consumes the wick and the oil.

title.en: Din and rachamim in Shammai and Hillel

summary.en: The Rav explains that Beis Shammai follow midas hadin and Beis Hillel midas harachamim, both 'divrei Elokim chaim', and that the halachah follows Beis Hillel because the world now runs with rachamim. He brings the Ramban that positive mitzvos come from love and negative ones from fear, and links Beis Shammai to the consuming blue of the flame and Beis Hillel to its illuminating white.

title.en: Pochet or mosif: start with aseh tov

summary.en: The Rav connects the dispute over decreasing or increasing the lights to sur mera and aseh tov: Beis Shammai put the guarding from sin first, Beis Hillel the doing of good. He brings the offerings of Kayin and Hevel and the wool and linen of kilayim, and says a Jew must not hold back from avodas Hashem because of his sins; he should begin with aseh tov and the sur mera will follow.

title.en: Enough oil for the whole road

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah light must shine into the public domain, the exile where most of a Jew's life goes to parnassah. The years of chinuch in yeshiva are the time to pour in enough oil, enough Torah and yiras Shamayim, so that it burns 'until the foot leaves the market' and lights his whole way.

title.en: Guarding other people's vineyards

summary.en: The Rav reads 'they made me a keeper of the vineyards, my own vineyard I did not keep' and laments talented Jewish young people who give themselves with mesiras nefesh for foreign causes and for peace, while Torah needs them. He says there will be no true peace until the days of Moshiach, and that the light of Torah must shine into the street.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the end of Niddah

summary.en: The Rav compares the last days of Chanukah to the last period in yeshiva and asks whether one has prepared enough Torah. He reads the end of Masechta Niddah on halichos and halachos, and through a teaching of Rabbi Shalom of Belz on 'beiso zo ishto' explains that a Jew's life outside the beis medrash must be run by the Torah.

title.en: A Chanina in every generation

summary.en: The Rav notes that Al Hanisim of Chanukah names Matisyahu's father Yochanan, and brings the Gemara that the whole world is fed for the sake of Chanina ben Dosa. He asks why the heavenly voice still says it generations later, and explains that in every generation there is a 'Chanina', a person who knows that all he has is a free gift and needs nothing for himself.

title.en: A life of miracles and the Chashmonaim

summary.en: The Rav explains why seeing 'Chanina' in a dream signals miracles: such a person sees even his bread and parnassah as a miracle, as Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa said that the One who told oil to burn can tell vinegar to burn. He explains that the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh came from knowing they had nothing, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: צד א: חיזוק מחנוכה - יש לי חלק באלקי ישראל!

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah was born of the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh, and that every Jew gains his share in it, and proclaims that he has a part in the G-d of Israel, through small daily acts of giving up his own will.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah lights is especially dear, and explains that Chanukah alone among the festivals came about through mesiras nefesh, which is what makes it dear. A Jew's share in Chanukah follows his own mesiras nefesh. He defines nefesh as a person's will, so mesiras nefesh means giving up one's will: not looking at what one should not see, holding back a cutting remark. He tells his listeners to join the Chashmonaim and to answer the Greeks, who demanded that Jews write that they have no part in the G-d of Israel, by declaring on every mitzvah that they do have a part. He then links the month of Teves to the Me'aras haMachpelah and to Avraham Avinu, who set aside his own comfort but never another's, and ends with a call to help others, with the mashal of the fruit tree and the cedar.

en: The Rambam calls only the mitzvah of Chanukah lights especially dear, because Chanukah alone was established through mesiras nefesh.
A Jew's share in Chanukah is in proportion to his own mesiras nefesh for Torah and Yiddishkeit.
Nefesh means a person's will, so mesiras nefesh is any act in which a Jew gives up his own will for Hashem.
Against the Greeks' demand to write that Jews have no part in the G-d of Israel, a Jew should declare through every mitzvah that he has a part.
Avraham Avinu set aside his own comfort, sitting out for guests three days after his milah, but never imposed on the comfort of others.
Chanukah is a time to help others grow in Torah, like a tree that gives fruit, without fearing that one's own growth will suffer.

title.en: Why Chanukah is called especially dear

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Rambam calls only the mitzvah of Chanukah lights especially dear, and explains that Chanukah is the one festival brought about by the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh; what comes through mesiras nefesh is precious.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh means giving up one's will

summary.en: The Rav says Chanukah is the time to remember the need for mesiras nefesh like the Chashmonaim, and that one's share in Chanukah follows it. He explains that nefesh means will, so mesiras nefesh is not only giving one's life but every act that goes against one's own will.

title.en: Torah as vessels; small acts of mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Rav explains that the words of Torah are vessels through which a Jew can grasp a holiness too great for creation to hold. He then gives everyday examples of mesiras nefesh: turning away from idle talk, not looking at what one should not see in the street, and holding back a sharp remark.

title.en: Joining the Chashmonaim: I have a part

summary.en: The Rav says all of Chanukah exists because of the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh, and urges each Jew to join them. He brings the Greeks' demand that Jews write they have no part in the G-d of Israel, and says a Jew should declare on his mezuzah, tefillin, Chanukah lights and tzitzis that he does have a part.

title.en: Teves and the Me'aras haMachpelah

summary.en: The Rav connects the month of Teves to the Me'aras haMachpelah, which was not destroyed as Yerushalayim was, and says something of the Avos in every Jew can never be destroyed. He tells how Avraham discovered the cave and saw that all tefillos go up from there.

title.en: Avraham: one's own comfort, not another's

summary.en: The Rav explains that a person may set aside only his own comfort, never someone else's. Avraham Avinu would not inconvenience others, yet three days after his milah, in pain, he sat out to welcome guests.

title.en: Spreading holiness and helping others

summary.en: The Rav says the Greeks wanted to take over the territory of holiness, while Jews set the Chanukah light in the public domain and founded holiness there. He calls on his listeners to help others, such as a friend who does not understand the shiur, and brings the mashal of the fruit tree and the cedar; he closes by asking them to draw strength from the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh.

catalogTitle: צד ב: מגודל אהבת הקב"ה אלינו הוא נותן לנו עוד זמן לשוב

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that out of His love Hashem extends the time for teshuvah past Yom Kippur until the last day of Chanukah, and that Chanukah calls on every Jew to renew himself through Torah and tefillah against the foreign culture entering his home.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the extensions of the time for teshuvah: the Gemara says tzaddikim are sealed on Rosh Hashanah while beinonim wait until Yom Kippur, the judgment is handed over only on Shemini Atzeres, and the chassidishe seforim bring from the Arizal that the time lasts until Zos Chanukah, an extension given for later, smaller generations. He counts the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah, 122, and shows the periods hinted in the number of pesukim of the parshiyos read then, with Ki Savo's 122 pesukim matching the full extension. Ki Savo belongs to the ending year, so it asks what was done with last year's 122 days, and he points to the hard events of the past year. Turning to Chanukah, he describes the Jews' mesirus nefesh against Greek ways, warns that today radio, newspapers, television and the internet bring the outside world into the home, and calls for kindling the lights of Torah. Through the reading of the nesiim, the Targum Yonasan and the Gemara in Sanhedrin he teaches that the real war is fought with Torah, tefillah and chessed, and ends with a call to use the extension to become a better Jew.

en: The time for teshuvah is extended in stages: Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, Yom Kippur for beinonim, Shemini Atzeres when the judgment is sent out, and Zos Chanukah, as the chassidishe seforim bring from the Arizal.
From Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah there are 122 days, and the stages of teshuvah are hinted in the number of pesukim of the parshiyos read in that season.
The extension until Chanukah was given because later, smaller generations could not finish their teshuvah by Yom Kippur as the great generations did.
Today the outside world, through radio, newspapers, television and the internet, has entered the Jewish home, and Chanukah calls for kindling the lights of Torah against it.
The war of the Jewish people is fought in every beis medrash, with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, as the Chashmonaim fought.

summary.en: The Rav lists how Hashem keeps extending the time for teshuvah: Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, Yom Kippur for beinonim, Shemini Atzeres, and, as the seforim bring from the Arizal, Zos Chanukah. He explains the last extension was given for later, smaller generations.

title.en: Counting 122 days and the hint in the parshiyos

summary.en: The Rav counts the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah and arrives at 122. He shows that the stages of teshuvah are hinted in the number of pesukim of the parshiyos read in this season, such as Haazinu's 52.

title.en: Ki Savo's 122 pesukim and the past year

summary.en: Someone pointed out to the Rav that Parshas Ki Savo has 122 pesukim. He asks why the hint is in the parsha of the tochachah and explains that it belongs to the ending year, asking what was done with last year's 122 days, and he recalls the painful events of the past year before calling for a fresh start.

title.en: Chanukah against the foreign culture at home

summary.en: The Rav describes the mesirus nefesh of the Jews against the Greeks for Torah and Yiddishkeit, warns against a Jew who learns and davens but whose outlook is goyish, and says that today radio, newspapers, television and the internet have turned the private home into a public domain. He ends with a call to kindle the lights of Torah.

title.en: The nesiim and the time of renewal

summary.en: The Rav explains why the parsha of the nesiim is read on Chanukah: the Mishkan was finished in Kislev but dedicated in Nissan, and Kislev received the Chanukah of the Chashmonaim. Chanukah is a time of chinuch and renewal like Rosh Hashanah, and he brings the Targum Yonasan that the nesiim read on Chanukah stand against the twelve princes of Yishmael.

title.en: The real war is in the beis medrash

summary.en: The Rav says the war of Yishmael against Klal Yisroel is not decided by weapons in Eretz Yisroel or Afghanistan but in every beis medrash, through Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, as the Chashmonaim fought. He brings the Gemara in Sanhedrin on being saved from chevlei Moshiach and closes with a call to use the extension until Zos Chanukah to become a better Jew, with a brachah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: ביכורים - Bringing the Fruit of ראשית to the Place of ראשית

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that bikurim, the first-ripened fruit, is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the place where creation began, and from there he builds a call to rise early in Elul and use the days of teshuvah before Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the mitzvah of bikurim and the idea that sparks of holiness are hidden in everything a person eats and uses, each one bound to his own nefesh. Through the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'hungry and thirsty' and the gifts of leket, shikchah and pe'ah, he shows that a thing reaches the person whose nature it matches. Rashi describes the fig that ripens first; such an early riser is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the first point of creation, and given to the kohanim, who are zerizim. Rosh Hashanah is the same beginning in time, so in Elul, the tired end of the year, one must wake up. He then lays out four periods of teshuvah, 30, 40, 52 and 122 days, hinted in the pesukim of Vayelech, Nitzavim and Haazinu, and reads the 122 pesukim of Ki Savo as rebuke for a past year whose days were wasted.

en: Every food, garment and possession holds sparks of holiness that belong to one specific person's nefesh, and only he can raise them by using it for Hashem.

Bikurim, the fruit that ripens before all others, is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the first place created, and given to the kohanim, who are zerizim, so that the early riser goes to the place and the people of early rising.

Rosh Hashanah is in time what the Beis HaMikdash is in space, the beginning; therefore Elul, the tired end of the year, is the time to wake up early and prepare, and one does not sleep on Rosh Hashanah.
There are four periods of teshuvah: 30 days to Rosh Hashanah, 40 to Yom Kippur, 52 to Shemini Atzeres according to the Zohar, and 122 to the last day of Chanukah according to the Arizal.
The 122 pesukim of Ki Savo, read before the new year, are rebuke about the past year: its 122 days of teshuvah were not used, and the Rav urges not to repeat that mistake.

title.en: Bikurim and the sparks in everything we use

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of the parsha about bringing the first fruits to the kohen, then introduces the idea that since Adam's sin sparks of holiness are imprisoned in all we eat, wear and live in, each bound to a particular person's nefesh.

title.en: Why people must be hungry and thirsty

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's explanation of 'hungry and thirsty': people must eat so that with their brachos they release the sparks in their food, which are an extension of their own nefesh, and he illustrates it with a shared apple and a lost pen.

title.en: Leket, shikchah and pe'ah fit the poor man

summary.en: The Rav explains that the gifts the Torah gives the poor carry the poor man's character: leket falls to the ground as he lies in the dust, shikchah is forgotten as he seems forgotten, and pe'ah is at the edge as he lives at the fringe of society.

title.en: The early fig goes to the place of beginning

summary.en: From Rashi's description of the fig that ripens first, the Rav explains that this 'early riser' is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the even shesiyah from which the world spread out, and given to the kohanim, who are zerizim.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, Elul and not sleeping

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rosh Hashanah is the beginning of time as the Beis HaMikdash is of space, while Elul is the tired end of the year when one must rise early. He brings Tehillim 92 on staying fresh in the house of Hashem, the Shulchan Aruch and the Rambam on not sleeping, and Yaakov's regret at sleeping at the place of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Forty days that decide the year

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Berachos that one may daven for a boy only during the first forty days, and applies it to the year: the thirty days of Elul and ten of Tishrei determine its character, like Moshe Rabbeinu's forty days ending on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Four periods of teshuvah: 30, 40, 52, 122

summary.en: The Rav lays out the Gemara on tzaddikim and beinonim, the Zohar's extension to Shemini Atzeres and the Arizal's to the last day of Chanukah, and, counting every month as thirty days, arrives at 30, 40, 52 and 122 days of teshuvah.

title.en: The hint in the parshiyos of teshuvah

summary.en: Seeking the periods of teshuvah in the parshiyos read in that season, the Rav explains why Vezos Habrachah is not counted and matches the pesukim of Vayelech, Nitzavim and Haazinu to the days, totaling 122. He relates that a listener once noted Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim and asks why that repetition is needed.

title.en: Ki Savo as rebuke for the past year

summary.en: The Rav answers that Ki Savo's 122 pesukim speak of the past year: its days of teshuvah were not used, and he lists the year's suffering and the growing impurity. He then stresses preparing to crown Hashem, who alone decides the fate of nations, whose leaders are puppets in His hands.

title.en: Wake up and use the days

summary.en: The Rav returns to the image of the sleeping figs, brings the Levi whose clothes were burnt for sleeping in the Beis HaMikdash, and urges using the 30, 40, 52 or 122 days. He tells the listeners that they are facing the Beis HaMikdash, the place from which teshuvah spreads, and closes with a brachah; a short exchange with listeners follows.

catalogTitle: אור המשיח נתגלה ע”י מסירת נפש (שייכות לפרשת וישב)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the light of Moshiach hidden in Chanukah and in Parshas Vayeshev is revealed only through mesirus nefesh, and that this is the bond between Vayeshev, Chanukah and Yud-Tes Kislev.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Maggid's demand that a ba'al korei know how each parsha connects to its week, and asks how Vayeshev connects to Yud-Tes Kislev. Chanukah, he explains, is the revelation of the hidden light of Moshiach: its mitzvah goes below ten tefachim into the public domain, to kindle souls that have fallen under the sitra achra. This is why the one Mishnah touching Chanukah speaks of a lamp placed below ten tefachim, and why Chanukah was little discussed until generations close to Moshiach. In Vayeshev the souls of both Moshiachs are hidden: Yehudah goes down, and Tamar waits until she is already burning before sending to him, because the Satan cannot stand against mesirus nefesh. Yosef, too, shows mesirus nefesh with Potiphar's wife, as did the Chashmonaim. The Rav closes with the mesirus nefesh of the Alter Rebbe, the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rayatz, and says a Jew today must have mesirus nefesh.

en: Chanukah is the revelation of the hidden light, the light of Moshiach, which every Jew carries within him in a concealed way.
Unlike the Shechinah, which never descended below ten tefachim, the Chanukah light goes below ten tefachim into the public domain to reach souls that have fallen under the sitra achra.
The souls of Moshiach ben Dovid and Moshiach ben Yosef are hidden in Parshas Vayeshev, in the descent of Yehudah and the birth of Peretz, and in Yosef's descent to Egypt.
The Satan cannot accuse against mesirus nefesh, so whoever brings Moshiach must have mesirus nefesh, as Tamar, Yehudah and Yosef did.
The Chanukah miracle itself came through the mesirus nefesh of the Chashmonaim, and a Jew who lights the Chanukah candle draws in the light of Moshiach.
The Chabad leaders, from the Alter Rebbe on, spread pnimiyus haTorah with mesirus nefesh, and this links Yud-Tes Kislev to Vayeshev and Chanukah.

title.en: The Maggid's ba'al korei and the question of Vayeshev

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Maggid of Mezritch asked the young Shneur Zalman whether he knew the connection of each parsha to its week before making him his ba'al korei, and asks what connects Parshas Vayeshev to Yud-Tes Kislev. He begins with the seforim's teaching that Chanukah reveals the light of Moshiach.

title.en: Chanukah goes below ten tefachim

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the Gemara that the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim with the Chanukah light, which is placed below ten tefachim in the public domain to kindle fallen souls with the hidden light. He then notes that the Mishnah and the early generations say almost nothing about Chanukah, unlike Purim, while the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Bnei Yissaschar speak of it at length.

title.en: Why Chanukah was hidden, and the one Mishnah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the hidden light of Chanukah stayed concealed in earlier generations, which were not yet close to Moshiach; Chanukah reaches even the 'refuse oils' that Shabbos cannot light, the souls Moshiach will gather from the ends of the heavens. He then explains why the Mishnah's only Chanukah law is the camel and the lamp below ten tefachim: that law holds the whole essence of Chanukah.

title.en: Moshiach's soul hidden in Vayeshev

summary.en: The Rav shows that the souls of both Moshiachs are hidden in Vayeshev: Yehudah goes down, and Peretz is born from Tamar in a concealed way so that there should be no accusation, illustrated with a parable of a man who hid his money in the thief's own sack. He then asks why Tamar waited until she was taken out to be burned before sending her proof to Yehudah.

title.en: Tamar's mesirus nefesh defeats the Satan

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the fire had already caught Tamar's garments when she sent to Yehudah, who admitted at once. He explains that the Satan had blocked Moshiach through Er and Onan, who later came back as Peretz and Zerach, so Tamar used the one thing the Satan cannot oppose, mesirus nefesh, and Yehudah accepted the shame with mesirus nefesh as well.

title.en: Yosef and the Chashmonaim: Moshiach through mesirus nefesh

summary.en: The Rav shows the same mesirus nefesh in Yosef, ancestor of Moshiach ben Yosef, who withstood Potiphar's wife's threats and fled without his garment. Both Moshiachs had to descend; the Chashmonaim likewise fought the mighty Greek kingdom with mesirus nefesh, and so Chanukah is the light of Moshiach that a Jew draws in when he lights the Chanukah candle.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe and the Tzemach Tzedek

summary.en: The Rav tells that the first Chassidic sefer, Toldos Yaakov Yosef, began the revelation of the Torah of Moshiach, pnimiyus haTorah, which aroused an accusation in heaven, and that the Alter Rebbe's deeper spreading of it led to his arrest in Russia, where he declared himself a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov and was accused of sending money to Eretz Yisroel. He then tells how the Tzemach Tzedek refused to sign a blank letter in Moscow and was let go.

title.en: The Rayatz, the shluchim, and mesirus nefesh today

summary.en: The Rav describes the Rayatz's mesirus nefesh in spreading Torah under the Communists and his demand that his chassidim do the same, and ties together Chanukah, Kislev, Vayeshev and Yud-Tes Kislev as days of mesirus nefesh. He mentions shluchim going to desolate places to kindle extinguished souls with the power of pnimiyus haTorah, says a Jew today must have mesirus nefesh, and closes with a brachah for the light of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: א: מסירת נפש על “ישראל גוי אחד בארץ”

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the name Yisrael, the oneness of 'goy echad', was earned through the mesiras nefesh of the sons of Yaakov at Shechem, the same mesiras nefesh of the Chashmonaim that Chanukah and its lamp at the door stand for.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the 613 mitzvos and seven rabbinic mitzvos corresponding to the 620 letters of the Aseres Hadibros, and the 600,000 letters of the Torah corresponding to the souls of Israel. Ner Chanukah, the last mitzvah, corresponds to the lowest Jew of the generation before Moshiach. He describes the mesiras nefesh of the Chashmonaim and of Chabad in Soviet Russia. He then asks why Yaakov received the name Yisrael only after Shechem, and brings the Divrei Yoel on why the people of Shechem accepted milah: to prevent a separate Jewish nation. The war of Shechem parallels the war of Chanukah; Chanukah's twenty-fifth day corresponds to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael, the acceptance of mesiras nefesh. After a story of Reb Naftali of Ropshitz, he explains Yaakov's setting of techumim and the Chanukah lamp at the door as a boundary between Israel and the nations, and closes with Chabad's shluchim.

en: Ner Chanukah, the last of the seven rabbinic mitzvos, corresponds to the lowest Jew, the souls of the generation before Moshiach.
The Chashmonaim went out to war with mesiras nefesh and no natural chance of success, trusting in the eternity of Israel and of the Torah.
The people of Shechem accepted milah because the wicked cannot bear a separate Jewish nation bound to Hashem, and wanted to assimilate it away.
The name Yisrael expresses the oneness of Israel with Hashem, and it was earned only through the mesiras nefesh of Shechem.
Chanukah, on its twenty-fifth day, is the yom tov of Shema Yisrael, which means accepting mesiras nefesh.
The Chanukah lamp placed at the doorway is a boundary between the domain of Israel and the public domain of the nations.

title.en: Shechem, Chanukah and Shema Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav draws the parallel between the war of the sons of Yaakov at Shechem and the war of the Chashmonaim against the Greeks, both for the holiness of the Jewish family, and explains that the twenty-fifth of Kislev corresponds to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael, the acceptance of mesiras nefesh.

title.en: Tzaddikim speak to Hashem: Reb Naftali's milk

summary.en: The Rav explains that when tzaddikim speak to people they are speaking to Hashem, and tells how Reb Naftali of Ropshitz demanded strong milk in his kitchen just before a nursing mother came for help. He applies this to the sons of Yaakov, whose words to Shechem were a plea to Hashem for a wall between Israel and the nations.

title.en: Techum Shabbos and the lamp at the door

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov's first act at Shechem was to set techumim: Shabbos is the private domain of oneness with Hashem, and assimilation is like carrying out into the public domain. The difference between Israel and the nations is like that between Shabbos and the weekdays, and the Chanukah lamp at the door marks that boundary.

title.en: The name Yisrael earned; Chabad's shluchim

summary.en: The Rav concludes that the name Yisrael was earned through the mesiras nefesh of Shechem, not at the meeting with the angel. He calls the Rebbes and chassidim of Chabad Yochanan Kohen Gadol and his soldiers, who keep sending shluchim even after shluchim were killed, and closes with a blessing.

catalogTitle: ב: אלקי אבטח בך

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that true bitachon means doing what Hashem wants without fear of loss or mockery, and shows that the Chashmonaim's victory, and the mitzvah of Chanukah itself, rest on this trust.

abstract.en: The Rav defines bitachon as doing the right thing with certainty that Hashem will not let one lose by it, and says anger is a sign of lacking emunah and bitachon, since no one can do good or harm without Hashem's will, as Dovid HaMelech showed when Shimi ben Gera cursed him. A Midrash about a man saved because he relied on being the king's relative explains 'Elokai becha batachti'. The test of bitachon is not fearing mockery: Chananiah, Mishael and Azariah were saved in the merit of Yaakov, whom the wicked mocked, and the Shulchan Aruch opens with not being ashamed before scoffers. The thirteen Chashmonaim, hopelessly outnumbered, went to war with bitachon and said 'Yoshev b'seser'. Chanukah, the last rabbinic mitzvah, belongs to the last generation, and its mitzvah, 'ner ish uveiso', is a mitzvah of the family, which leads to an appeal for hachnasas kallah.

en: Bitachon means doing what is right with certainty that Hashem will not let one lose by it; one who expects to regret it later has no bitachon.
Anger is a sign that a person lacks emunah and bitachon, since no one can do good or harm without Hashem's will.
The test of bitachon is not being impressed by mockery when doing Hashem's will, which is why the Shulchan Aruch opens with not being ashamed before scoffers.
The Chashmonaim, outnumbered in every way, went to war with bitachon that Hashem would not let the Torah be uprooted, and said 'Yoshev b'seser', a psalm of pure bitachon.
Chanukah is the last mitzvah the Rabbanan instituted, and belongs to the last souls of the generation before Moshiach, who should strengthen themselves even when they see little merit in themselves.
The mitzvah of Chanukah, 'ner ish uveiso', is placed on the family rather than on the individual, and like a family it grows from day to day.

title.en: Bitachon, anger and the king's relative

summary.en: The Rav defines bitachon as acting with certainty that Hashem will not let one lose, calls anger a sign of missing emunah, and brings Dovid HaMelech's response to Shimi ben Gera. He then tells the Midrash's parable of a man spared because he relied on being the king's relative, explaining 'Elokai becha batachti'.

title.en: The test of bitachon: not fearing mockery

summary.en: The Rav calls the true test of bitachon knowing that Hashem wants one's service despite trials and ridicule, and brings the Midrash on Chananiah, Mishael and Azariah, who were saved from the fire in the merit of Yaakov, whom the wicked mocked.

title.en: The Chashmonaim went to war with bitachon

summary.en: The Rav shows that the Shulchan Aruch opens with not being ashamed before scoffers, then describes the thirteen Chashmonaim, outnumbered in every way, going to war trusting that Hashem would not let the Torah be uprooted. They said 'Yoshev b'seser', a psalm of bitachon that mentions no merit, and this, he says, is the idea of Chanukah.

title.en: The last mitzvah and the mitzvah of the family

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, the last rabbinic mitzvah, belongs to the last generation, and that 'ner ish uveiso' makes it a mitzvah of the family that grows each day. He closes by linking this to the gathering for hachnasas kallah and wishes a joyous Chanukah.

catalogTitle: The 6th Month Corresponds to the 6th אושפיזין - Yosef הצדיק

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Elul, the sixth month, corresponds to Yosef HaTzaddik, the sixth of the ushpizin, who embodies Seder Taharos, so that Elul is the month of purity that prepares for the holiness of Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'lachazos b'noam Hashem', said in Elul, and the bond of 'ani l'dodi v'dodi li'. Following the Arizal, the seven months from Nissan to Tishrei correspond to the seven ushpizin, so Elul is Yosef's month. He then asks why Yaakov taught Yosef only five orders of Mishnah, as the Baal HaTurim reads 'zekunim', and why Yaakov, unlike Avraham, needed teachers at all. He builds an answer from the stages of Klal Yisrael: the avos and the seven ro'im are single trunks, the shevatim are branches. Yosef was a ro'eh, not a shevet, and corresponds to Seder Taharos, which he knew by himself. Avraham, the first, contains all the days. Yosef's purity explains how Yaakov sensed him in the produce from Mitzrayim, his title 'tzaddik', and the special quality of Mishkan Shiloh. Elul, Yosef's taharah, prepares for Rosh Hashanah's kedusha, and the Rav urges using the forty days.

en: Following the Arizal, the seven months from Nissan to Tishrei correspond to the seven ushpizin, so Elul, the sixth month, is the month of Yosef.
The avos and the seven ro'im are single units, trunks of the tree, while the twelve shevatim are branches; Yosef was not a shevet but one of the seven ro'im.
Each of the seven ro'im corresponds to a day of the week and an order of Mishnah, with Yosef, the sixth, corresponding to Seder Taharos.
Yaakov taught Yosef only five orders, as the word 'zekunim' hints, because Yosef knew Seder Taharos by himself.
Yaakov sensed that Yosef was alive in Mitzrayim from the purity, the taste and fragrance, of the produce that Yosef personally handled.
Elul, Yosef's month of taharah, is the preparation for Rosh Hashanah, because purity must come before holiness.

title.en: Elul, the sixth month, and Yosef

summary.en: The Rav reads 'lachazos b'noam Hashem' as a wish that Hashem have nachas from us, and describes Elul as the time of 'ani l'dodi v'dodi li'. He then states that Elul is the sixth month and, following the Arizal, corresponds to Yosef, the sixth of the ushpizin.

title.en: Ben zekunim and the missing Taharos

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's two explanations of 'ben zekunim', the second being that Yaakov passed on to Yosef all the Torah he had received. He then brings the Baal HaTurim's hint that 'zekunim' spells five orders of Mishnah, and asks where Seder Taharos is.

title.en: Avraham knew Torah by instinct

summary.en: The Rav explains Chazal's statement that Avraham's kidneys taught him Torah: he knew the whole Torah by instinct, as animals know what is in their nature. He asks why Yaakov, the choicest of the avos, needed teachers, and asks too why Yaakov sensed that Yosef was in Mitzrayim only at that point.

title.en: Trunk and branches: avos, shevatim, seven shepherds

summary.en: The Rav describes the stages of Klal Yisrael: single avos, then twelve shevatim as branches of Yaakov's trunk, then seventy souls, then a nation. On the three regalim the shevatim return to their trunk, and the seven ro'im, the ushpizin, are units who sustain every Jew; he notes the two orders of the ushpizin.

title.en: Twelve paths and seven: the future elevation

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the twelve paths of Krias Yam Suf with the seven streams of the future split in Yeshaya 11, when the shevatim will be raised to the level of the ro'im and the strife of Ephraim and Yehuda will end. He compares the twelve weekday requests of Shemoneh Esrei to Shabbos's single brachah, and Musaf of Rosh Chodesh to the unity of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Yosef a ro'eh, not a shevet; Chok LeYisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yosef was one of the seven ro'im, not a shevet, so Ephraim and Menashe took his place; the brothers mistook his higher conduct for arrogance, and Rashi's reading of 'even Yisrael' as father and son shows he had the quality of an av. He then describes the Chok LeYisrael order of the Arizal, matching each day to one of the ro'im and an order of Mishnah.

title.en: The first contains all: why Taharos is missing

summary.en: The Rav explains that Avraham, as the first, 'ba bayamim', comes with all the days, so he knew the whole Torah by himself, while Yitzchak knew only Seder Moed and the shevatim had to be taught everything. This answers the Baal HaTurim's question: Yaakov did not need to teach Yosef Taharos, and he loved him because he had to teach him less.

title.en: Each av and his order of Mishnah

summary.en: The Rav goes through the correspondences: Avraham is Zeraim and emunah, which is why Zeraim opens with Brachos; Yitzchak is Moed; Yaakov is Nashim, as seen in his toil for his wives; Nezikin, which sharpens the mind, belongs to Moshe; and Kodashim to Aharon.

title.en: Taharah gives taste and fragrance

summary.en: The Rav explains that David is the hidden 'sod' of Shabbos, and brings the end of Sotah that when taharah was taken away, produce lost its taste and fragrance. Yosef is taharah: produce he handled in Mitzrayim carried a holy fragrance, and from it Yaakov knew that Yosef was alive, uniting Rashi's and Targum Yonasan's readings of 'vayar Yaakov'.

title.en: Yosef the tzaddik and Potiphar's wife

summary.en: The Rav explains why only Yosef carries the title 'tzaddik': a seventeen-year-old torn from his father's home, he withstood Potiphar's wife for a whole year. He retells from Chazal her threats and his answers from pesukim, ending with 'Hashem ohev tzaddikim'.

title.en: Mishkan Shiloh, the Mishkan of Yosef

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Mishkan Shiloh, in Yosef's territory, with the Beis HaMikdash in Yerushalayim: Shiloh was temporary, but kodashim could be eaten wherever it could be seen, a merit of Yosef's guarding his eyes. He returns to Elul as the sixth month corresponding to Yosef and Tishrei as the seventh, David and malchus.

title.en: Elul prepares: taharah before kedusha

summary.en: As Friday prepares for Shabbos, Elul prepares for Rosh Hashanah; the Rav brings the Likutei Torah that in Elul the King is in the field and anyone may approach him. Taharah precedes kedusha, and he brings the Gemara on the dudaim, pure young men or baalei teshuvah, and the fragrance of the ketores that was smelled at Shiloh.

title.en: The forty days and closing brachah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur absorbed the teshuvah of Moshe's last forty days on the mountain, and calls on listeners to use them. The thirty days of Elul are Shiloh and the ten days are Yerushalayim, with Rosh Hashanah as the Beis HaMikdash of time; he closes with a brachah for a good year.

catalogTitle: “ה' אלקי יגיה חשכי” - האור הגנוז מאיר בתוך החושך

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah light is the hidden light (or haganuz) that Hashem sends down into the deepest darkness, as it came down to Yosef in Egypt, and that Zos Chanukah, which includes the whole of Chanukah, is a day of emunah and of thanking Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the difference between the private domain, the domain of Hashem, and the public domain: Chanukah is lit at the door, where the Jew goes out into the long night of exile, and there Hashem sends the hidden light. He applies this to the descent into Egypt: Yocheved, Serach and above all Yosef, whom no one recognized because he was the hidden light. On the day of Yosef's test, the idolaters' festival, he could not be saved by Torah, so the Kisei HaKavod came down to him; the Rav suggests that day was Chanukah, near the tekufah. Yosef is a sign for his children that in the worst darkness Hashem holds a Jew's hand: 'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki'. Zos Chanukah, the final sealing after Rosh Hashanah, includes all the lights and is for those who live by emunah alone. He ends with thanking Hashem, coming on time to davening, and a brachah.

en: The Chanukah light is lit at the door because it belongs to the place where a Jew goes out from Hashem's private domain into the public domain of darkness, and there Hashem sends down the hidden light.
A Jew who finds himself in darkness should take Chanukah along and know that the hidden light is concealed in that darkness; when he believes it, it is revealed.
Yosef was the hidden light, which is why no one recognized him, and in his double darkness in Egypt the Kisei HaKavod came down to him.
Yosef is a sign for his children: even when a Jew cannot hold on to a word of davening or learning, Hashem holds his hand in the middle of the darkness.
Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, includes the whole of Chanukah and is the final sealing for those who were not sealed on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Chanukah is a time of thanks: the Rav says a Jew should fix in himself the belief that Hashem does far more for him than he deserves, and take on to thank Him for every small thing.

title.en: Chanukah at the door of the public domain

summary.en: The Rav says every matter is tied to its time, and contrasts the private domain, Hashem's domain, with the public domain. The Chanukah light belongs at the door where Klal Yisrael goes out into the long night of exile, and there Hashem sends the hidden light, as in 'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki'.

title.en: Taking Chanukah into the darkness; Yosef unrecognized

summary.en: The Rav says a Jew who finds himself in darkness should remember that the hidden light is concealed there. The descent to Egypt needed such a light: Yocheved, born at the entrance, and Serach, who brought Yaakov the good news; and Yosef, who was the hidden light and therefore was not recognized.

title.en: Yosef's double darkness and the Kisei HaKavod

summary.en: The Rav explains that on the day of Yosef's test he was in a place of darkness and a time of darkness, the idolaters' festival, and could not protect himself through Torah; so the Kisei HaKavod came down to him. Yosef became the vessel for the hidden light, and the Rav ties the thirty-six Chanukah lights to the thirty-six tzaddikim, with Yosef at their head.

title.en: Yosef's test fell on Chanukah

summary.en: After saying that some matters are better not thought about, the Rav explains that on Chanukah one goes out into the public domain, and that whatever exists in holiness has its opposite. He suggests that the day of Yosef's test, near the winter tekufah, was Chanukah, and connects the twenty-fifth day with the twenty-fifth letter missing from 'Baruch Shem'.

title.en: Yosef as a sign: Hashem holds the hand in the dark

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yosef, left without Torah to save him, became a sign for his children: when Jews in the worst times cannot hold on to a word of davening or learning, Hashem still holds their hand. He brings the Midrash that darkness is Greece and explains 'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki' with a parable of a commentary written on a hard sefer; then he ties 'kehayom hazeh' to the twenty-fifth of Kislev.

title.en: Zos Chanukah: the final sealing that includes all

summary.en: The Rav brings the seforim and the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah is the final sealing of Rosh Hashanah, and contrasts the light of the eighth day with the darkness of the nations' new year. The eight nights correspond to the attributes of mercy that are 'mazal', above merit, for those who live by emunah; the eighth day is like the Holy of Holies and includes all, as all the Nesi'im are read.

title.en: Burning the wicks; Chanukah as thanks

summary.en: The Rav describes the custom of burning all the leftover wicks and oil on Zos Chanukah, showing that the day includes the whole Chanukah. He says its avodah is a bit of emunah that every Jew is a tzaddik, and that Chanukah is for thanks: one can never thank Hashem enough, and the eight days teach a Jew to thank Him for every small thing.

title.en: Coming on time to davening; closing brachah

summary.en: The Rav asks people to come on time to davening and say Hodu with the minyan, mentions Jews who need yeshuos and a segulah of saying Ketores with the tzibbur, and adds his own segulah of saying Hodu together with the minyan. He ends with taking on to thank Hashem, the bond of davening and learning, and a brachah that the darkness flee and the light of the eighth candle shine.

catalogTitle: צד א: יום של אמונה בדברים שהם למעלה מהשגתינו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, and above all Zos Chanukah, comes from a realm above human understanding, so its light and its good sealing for the Jewish people rest on their simple emunah in what they cannot grasp.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara's question 'Mai Chanukah', asked of no other Yom Tov, and explains that the answer, eight days, is itself the point: eight is above the seven days of nature, and Chanukah comes from a world one may ask about but cannot know. He finds this in the name Chashmonaim, made of shemen, the letter ches and 'mai', and in oil, which always rises. With a mashal of a king who jumps into the mud for his child, he explains why this light still descends below ten handbreadths, the one Chanukah law hinted in the Mishnah. The miracle broke the Greek demand to understand everything. Through the Ramban, the Chiddushei HaRim and the Bnei Yissaschar he shows that the hidden light of Chanukah never goes out, like Shemini Atzeres. Zos Chanukah completes the Rosh Hashanah judgment, and Hashem then finds hidden merits in every Jew, as the Imrei Emes teaches from Parshas Mikeitz.

en: Chanukah lasts eight days, and eight stands above the seven days of nature, so Chanukah comes from a realm one cannot understand.
Greek wisdom held that one believes only what one understands, and the Chanukah miracle broke that impurity through simple emunah.
The light of Chanukah is the hidden light that is never extinguished, and in it lies the eternity of the Jewish people.
The judgment that begins on Rosh Hashanah comes from the hidden world and is completed on Zos Chanukah.
Jews merit a good sealing on Zos Chanukah because they believe in Hashem and in things they cannot understand.
On Zos Chanukah Hashem finds hidden merits in every Jew, merits even the greatest angels could not find.
