title.en: Why the Gemara asks 'Mai Chanukah'

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Gemara asks 'what is Chanukah' about no other Yom Tov, and explains that its answer, eight days, shows Chanukah comes from a realm above nature that one may ask about but cannot know. This is why Jews are sealed for good on Zos Chanukah without a reason one can explain.

title.en: Chashmonaim, oil, and the king's child

summary.en: The Rav reads the name Chashmonaim as shemen, ches and 'mai', and explains that oil always rises above, belonging to the realm of eight. With a mashal of a king who jumps into the mud to save his child, he explains why the Shechinah nevertheless descends below ten handbreadths on Chanukah.

title.en: The one Chanukah law in the Mishnah

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Mishnah contains no Chanukah laws except one deduced from it, that the Chanukah light belongs below ten handbreadths, and connects this to Rebbi, of the house of Dovid and the aspect of Moshiach. He then explains that Greek wisdom demanded understanding everything, and the miracle from the realm above reason broke that impurity.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the eternal menorah

summary.en: The Rav says the eighth day is the answer to 'Mai Chanukah', and in it lies Hashem's love for the Jewish people and the secret of their eternity. He brings Rashi and the Ramban on Beha'alosecha, that Aharon was told his share is forever, and the Chiddushei HaRim, that Aharon's menorah was hidden still burning.

title.en: The eighth is never nullified

summary.en: Bringing the Bnei Yissaschar that the Chanukah lights shine with the hidden light, the Rav compares Chanukah to Shemini Atzeres, whose blessing stays because the eighth is above this world. He then connects Chanukah to Rosh Hashanah through the verse 'beyond the river your fathers dwelt from olam', reading olam as the hidden world.

title.en: 'Lo chen haresha'im': belief in the hidden

summary.en: From 'kein asah es hamenorah' and the Midrash on 'lo chen haresha'im', the Rav explains that the wicked, followers of Greek wisdom, deny what they cannot see, while Jews believe in Hashem, the Torah and the Chanukah miracle. For that emunah alone they are sealed for good, and the wicked have no standing in that judgment.

title.en: Hashem finds merits: the Imrei Emes on Mikeitz

summary.en: The Rav brings the Imrei Emes on 'HaElokim matza es avon avadecha': the shevatim were so pure that even their fault had to be searched for and 'found'. Through Rashi's kal vachomer in that parshah he explains that if this is so for judgment, how much more Hashem searches out and finds hidden merits in every Jew in the week of Chanukah.

title.en: The hidden light in every Jew; rejoicing and thanks

summary.en: The Rav concludes that on Zos Chanukah the hidden light in every Jew comes out and by its light his merit is written for good. He calls for joy in Zos Chanukah and in emunah, and asks everyone to come on time to daven the next morning and say Hallel together, thanking Hashem for all the mitzvos and minhagim of Chanukah.

title.en: Blessing: the seal of the Kohen Gadol

summary.en: The Rav blesses the gathering with a good sealing, describing Hashem as the Kohen Gadol whose seal the Greeks could not touch, and every Jew sealed on Zos Chanukah with the seal of oil. The recording ends with singing that the ASR could not transcribe.

catalogTitle: The Current פרשיות Allude to the גמר החתימה (Explanation of the Concept of פקידה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows how the sedros read in the season of teshuvah hint at the four periods of judgment, from Rosh Hashanah until Zos Chanukah, and calls on his listeners to build protection for Klal Yisrael in a coming year of pekidah.

abstract.en: The Rav lists four judgment periods from Rosh Chodesh Elul: 30 days to Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, 40 to Yom Kippur for beinonim, 52 to Shemini Atzeres, and 122 to Zos Chanukah. Nitzavim (40 pesukim), Vayeilech (30) and Haazinu (52) hint at them, and together they make 122, as does Ki Savo. He explains that Ki Savo reproaches the wasted 122 days of last year, while the coming 122 are only hinted, out of respect for Klal Yisrael. As a sample, he finds both orders of the ushpizin in Haazinu's 48th and 50th pesukim. He then contrasts Sukkos, holy like the Beis HaMikdash and above ten tefachim, with Chanukah, below ten. Turning to the coming year, Tav Shin Samach, a year of pekidah, he explains why such years were often tragic, points to hopeful signs, and urges teshuvah and Torah as Klal Yisrael's true protection.

en: There are four periods of judgment counted from Rosh Chodesh Elul: 30 days to Rosh Hashanah, 40 to Yom Kippur, 52 to Shemini Atzeres and 122 to Zos Chanukah.
The pesukim of Nitzavim (40), Vayeilech (30) and Haazinu (52) match these periods, and together they make 122.
Ki Savo's 122 pesukim reproach last year's unused 122 days, while the coming 122 days are hinted only through a combination of sedros, out of respect for Klal Yisrael.
The sukkah carries the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash and stays above ten tefachim, while Chanukah is its opposite: below ten, in the public domain, in the dark nights of Teves.
The coming year, Tav Shin Samach, is a year of pekidah, yet nobody knows when Mashiach will come, and such years were often tragic because the Satan accuses.
Each Yom Tov gives a gift for the year, and Sukkos gives protection; those who learn Torah and do teshuvah must supply that protection for Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Four periods of judgment

summary.en: The Rav lays out four periods for teshuvah counted from Rosh Chodesh Elul: Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, Yom Kippur for beinonim, Shemini Atzeres according to the Zohar, and Zos Chanukah according to the Bas Ayin. He counts 122 days to Zos Chanukah, taking Cheshvan as 30 days.

title.en: Nitzavim, Vayeilech and Haazinu count the days

summary.en: The Rav shows that Vayeilech's 30 pesukim, Nitzavim's 40 and Haazinu's 52 match the periods, explains why Nitzavim comes first, and excludes Vezos Habrachah. Together they make 122, and his son-in-law added that Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim.

title.en: Ki Savo: last year's 122 days

summary.en: The Rav asks why the 122 is hinted twice and why it is not stated in one sedra. He answers that Ki Savo, the sedra of the curses that ends the old year, reproaches the 122 days of last year that were not used, and calls to use the coming days for teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.

title.en: Why the coming 122 days are only hinted

summary.en: The Rav explains that the three sedros state 30, 40 and 52 clearly, but the 122 days ahead are only hinted, because needing so long is a disgrace, just as Rashi says Moshe gave his rebuke by hint out of respect for Klal Yisrael. He adds that he found hints for many single days in single pesukim.

title.en: The ushpizin in Haazinu's pesukim

summary.en: As a sample, the Rav brings the two orders of the ushpizin in the Zohar, by middos and by chronology, followed by Chassidim and Ashkenazim. He shows that the 48th pasuk of Haazinu names Moshe and hints at Yosef as 'etzem', and the 50th names Aharon and hints at Yosef, so both orders have their hint.

title.en: Sukkah above ten, Chanukah below ten

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Sukkos and Chanukah: a sukkah must be ten tefachim high, learned in the Gemara from the kapores and the rule that the Shechinah never descended below ten, while the Chanukah light belongs below ten. Though the conclusion is a halachah l'Moshe miSinai, he explains that even the Gemara's first thought is Torah and shows a bond between the sukkah and the Kodesh HaKodashim.

title.en: The sukkah as the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Rav calls Sukkos the high point of Tishrei and Shemini Atzeres its peak, citing the Chasam Sofer. The sefarim say the sukkah has the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash, so one should keep it holy, yet as 'the heavenly mother' it takes a person in whatever state he is; on Shemini Atzeres the sukkah comes into the house.

title.en: Chanukah in the realm of darkness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah is the opposite of the sukkah: its mitzvah is in the public domain, below ten tefachim, on the left side of the door, in the long nights of Teves, the domain of the sitra achra. He reads 'Haazinu hashamayim' as the holy days up to Sukkos and 'v'sishma ha'aretz' as Chanukah, when the Shechinah comes down to the earth.

title.en: Sukkos gives protection; the year Tav Shin Samach

summary.en: The Rav explains that each Yom Tov is a reservoir for the year: Pesach gives geulah, Shavuos Torah, and Sukkos protection, as in 'ufros aleinu sukkas shlomecha'. He then turns to the much-discussed coming year, Tav Shin Samach, stressing that nobody knows when Mashiach will come.

title.en: Pekidah, and nobody knows the end

summary.en: The Rav explains pekidah: years in which Hashem considers bringing Mashiach, which can be found from pesukim and Gemara, yet they are not certainly the year. He brings that Yaakov could not reveal the end, a year in the Gemara that passed, the Rambam's signs of Mashiach, and the story of Bar Koziva whom Rabbi Akiva thought was Mashiach.

title.en: Why years of pekidah were tragic, and signs of hope

summary.en: The Rav explains that years of pekidah were often tragic because the Satan, fearing Mashiach, accuses Klal Yisrael, and gives examples: Tav Ches with the decrees of Chmielnicki, the Malbim's year 1914, and Tav Shin. From the words of Manoach's wife he argues that the great things happening now, Jews gathered in Eretz Yisrael and learning Torah, show Hashem's favor and a beginning of the ingathering.

title.en: The true defenders of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav says the coming year needs protection, and Hashem expects it from those who learn Torah and do mitzvos: teshuvah builds the sukkah, they are the true defense force, and the four minim, the letters of Hashem's Name, are their weapons. He urges trying again for Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkos, and closes with a blessing for a year of teshuvah, simchah and geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Eliyahu HaNavi, though from the tribe of Binyamin, is called a kohen, and how lighting the Chanukah candles and a bris bring every Jew into the state of a kohen, as it will be in the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Harachaman of a bris that calls Eliyahu HaNavi 'kohen tzedek', and asks how one may pray with a title that is not true. The Midrash disputes whether Eliyahu was from Gad or Binyamin, and Eliyahu himself said he descends from Rachel. When asked in the Gemara why he stood in a cemetery of gentiles if he is a kohen, he answered with Rabbi Shimon's view, which we do not follow; Tosafos says he was only deflecting. The Rav then brings that Chanukah lights keep their power all year and make the home a Beis HaMikdash, and explains that the lighter becomes a kohen, since the light of Moshiach is revealed and in the future every Jew will be a kohen. Eliyahu, who always lives in the atmosphere of Moshiach, is therefore always a kohen and paskens like Rabbi Shimon. He ends with the bris as a korban and blessings for the family.

en: Eliyahu HaNavi was not a kohen by lineage: he himself said he descends from Rachel, and Tosafos says his answer about Rabbi Shimon's view was only a deflection.
The power and impression of the Chanukah lights remain in the home all year, and the Jewish home becomes a Beis HaMikdash.
The Rav explains that whoever lights Chanukah candles becomes a kohen, because the light of Moshiach is revealed then and in the future every Jew will be a kohen.
Eliyahu, the herald of the redemption, always lives in the state of the days of Moshiach, so he is always a kohen and rules like Rabbi Shimon as the halacha will be in the future.
A bris is like a korban, and when Eliyahu comes to it he brings the atmosphere of Moshiach, so every Jew there carries a spark of kehunah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every generation's new answer to how the first night of Chanukah was a miracle draws down a new salvation, and that for our empty, fallen generation the miracle is lit even from an empty flask with only a trace of oil left on its walls.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the repetition, in Parshas Beha'aloscha, of how the menorah was made as one beaten piece, and turns to the well-known question of what the miracle of the first night was. He brings the Tzvi LaTzaddik and the Yismach Yisroel, who answer that the flask found was empty, holding only drops left on its walls. Asking how a new answer can differ from all the Rishonim, he explains through the Mishnah in Niddah and the Arizal that each Torah view reflects its own heavenly heichal, and that each chacham's chiddush on the Chanukah miracle draws down a new salvation. Chanukah, he says, is above all for the lowly later generations, which are like empty ears of grain. Leaders shrink, yet Hashem can be served in every situation, and today a sigh of teshuvah counts as much as great fasts did once. In our generation there is no flask, only a trace of oil, and that suffices. On Zos Chanukah he explains the menorah as one piece, joining even its base, the souls of the end of days, to its lights.

en: The Tzvi LaTzaddik and the Yismach Yisroel answer that the flask the Chashmona'im found was empty, used before for oil, and the few drops left on it made even the first night a miracle.
Each Torah view comes from its own heichal in Heaven according to the root of the scholar's soul, and the psak decided below shapes reality in this world.
Every chacham's new answer to how the Chanukah miracle happened draws down a new salvation in his generation.
Chanukah is mainly for the later, lower generations, who are like empty ears of grain, and its light comes down to them.
Following the Beis Aharon and the Ba'al Shem Tov, Hashem can and must be served in every situation, with whatever one has.
In today's small generations a sigh of teshuvah or a resolution to improve is as great before Hashem as the hard avodah of earlier times.
The menorah, made as one beaten piece down to its base, shows that all of Klal Yisroel, even the souls of the end of days, are one with its shining lights.

title.en: Many true answers: the heichalos above

summary.en: The Rav asks how many conflicting answers can all be true, and brings the Mishnah in Niddah where Rashi, Tosafos and the Rambam explain differently and the Chasam Sofer writes that reality matches only the Rambam. He answers with the Arizal and the Beis Yosef on the shape of the letters, and with the teaching that in Heaven there are many heichalos, each learning Torah according to its own middos.

title.en: Psak shapes reality; each answer brings a new salvation

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rashi and Tosafos each spoke from their own root, while the Rambam as a posek matched this world, and that reality follows the psak. So every chacham who answers the Beis Yosef's question draws down a new kind of miracle in his generation. He adds that Chanukah is mainly for the later generations and for those too low to rise to Shabbos.

title.en: Falling generations and the empty ears of grain

summary.en: The Rav says that the lower the generation falls, the nearer Moshiach comes, citing 'nafla velo sosif' and the Chessed l'Avraham. Today's generations are like Pharaoh's empty ears of grain, and as Yosef brought plenty into the years of famine, Chanukah sweetens the season of Teves. He describes the emptiness of the individual compared with the avodah of earlier generations.

title.en: Shrinking leaders; serving Hashem in every situation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the navi was once called ro'eh because a look from the tzaddik was enough, later speech was needed, and today even speech does not help. He brings the Beis Aharon's Yiddish teaching that no creature can raise itself to serve G-d except as He wills, and the Ba'al Shem Tov's lesson that one serves Hashem in every circumstance, even with confusion during davening.

title.en: Stories: locked in, and a teaching that lasted three years

summary.en: The Rav tells of a man locked in a place where one may not think words of Torah, who knocked on the walls for hours so as not to think Torah, as his way of serving Hashem there. He then tells of a chassid who came to the Beis Aharon after three years because one short teaching had sustained him until then, and the Rebbe wrote it down.

title.en: Then and now: a sigh of teshuvah suffices

summary.en: The Rav tells, as heard from the Skverer Rebbe, of a boy who rested from learning by learning complex Mishnayos and Hilchos Kiddush HaChodesh, and did not know what playing meant; such children no longer grow today. He brings the Beis Aharon on 'dor ledor yeshabach' and the Arizal's answer about Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's fast: in small generations a sigh to Hashem counts as much.

title.en: No flask today, only a trace of oil

summary.en: The Rav explains that earlier generations still had a pure flask, often a tzaddik of the generation, but today there is not even that, only a little oil clinging to the walls. In our generation, he says, the chachamim revealed a new Chanukah miracle from an empty flask, and the seal that remains is the point of emunah of Avraham Avinu, whom the Midrash calls a Kohen Gadol, which no Greek can defile.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the empty eighth light

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al HaTanya that the lights reach even the 'feet', those who still long for Hashem. He explains that the eighth light stood empty all of Chanukah and is lit only now, that each night corresponds to one of the thirteen middos of mercy, and that the gathering in shul allows lighting even later.

title.en: The menorah as all of Klal Yisroel, one piece

summary.en: The Rav explains that on the eighth day Beha'aloscha is read because the menorah includes all of Klal Yisroel and the whole Torah. The seven shepherds shine at its top, and its base is the souls of the end of days, yet all is one beaten piece. He says this parsha speaks of the Chanukah menorah and so repeats that even the base is mikshah.

title.en: Gam yachad: gathering as one, and a prayer for the end

summary.en: The Rav explains the psalm said before lighting, 'Hinei mah tov… gam yachad': the Chanukah gathering is itself mikshah, and the good oil flows from the head to the beard, the thirteen middos. He closes with a prayer that the empty souls of the end of days be helped and the whole menorah be complete.

oneLiner.en: At the seudah of Zos Chanukah the Rav explains that Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon and the kohanim, the day of hod and hallel, on which every Jew, by lighting his candles, builds a piece of the menorah of the Beis Hamikdash that Moshiach will bring down.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's question why the menorah follows the offerings of the nesi'im, and with the Ramban's answer that Aharon's portion is the Chanukah lights. Chanukah is therefore the Yom Tov of Aharon and the kohanim, when every Jewish home becomes a Beis Hamikdash, and its eight lights correspond to the names of Moshiach. The seudah of Zos Chanukah strengthens the emunah in Moshiach and the waiting for him. Aharon is the middah of hod, and so Chanukah is the day of thanks and hallel; the Rav connects Hallel to Aharon's years and to the Beis Hamikdash. Each generation, lighting its candles, builds a part of the menorah of the third Beis Hamikdash: the great generations the cups and flowers, our low generation the base, all one hammered piece, as the Tanya teaches of all souls. He closes with the chasimah of Zos Chanukah and a tefilah for the redemption.

en: Following the Ramban, the Rav explains that Aharon's consolation was the Chanukah lights, so Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon and the kohanim.
Through the Chanukah lights Aharon inaugurates every Jewish home as a Beis Hamikdash.
The seudah of Zos Chanukah is meant to strengthen the emunah in Moshiach and the hope for the yeshuah.
Aharon is the middah of hod, and Chanukah, which is in hod, is the day of thanks and Hallel.
Every generation, by lighting Chanukah candles, builds a part of the menorah of the future Beis Hamikdash, which will come down from Heaven when it is complete.
The lowest generations make the base of the menorah, yet the menorah is one hammered piece, binding the lowest Jew to the highest.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that Ki Savo is read before Rosh Hashanah so the year ends with its curses. He then lays out four stages of judgment: tzaddikim are sealed on Rosh Hashanah, beinonim on Yom Kippur, others wait until Hoshana Rabbah and Shemini Atzeres, and the last until Zos Chanukah. These are hinted in the pesukim: Nitzavim has 40, Vayelech 30 and Haazinu 52, together 122, the number of days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah. Since Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim, he explains that it speaks of last year's 122 days, which were wasted, and the tragedies of the past year followed. Nitzavim's 40, Vayelech's 30 and Haazinu's 52 pesukim match the stages, and together make 122, the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah.

The threat of Yishmael is sharpest now because the Satan, knowing that the fall of Yishmael brings his own end and the end of the galus, fights hardest just before Mashiach.
The tefillos and kriah of Rosh Hashanah center on Mashiach, the return of Tziyon's children, and the banishment of Yishmael from Eretz Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk in Beha'aloscha about Aharon lighting the Menorah and its being 'mikshah', and asks why the Torah repeats this. He then asks why the minhag is one menorah of eight lamps rather than a separate lamp each night. From the Gemara's two versions of the Chanukah brachah he draws two sides of the miracle: salvation for Klal Yisrael and downfall of the nations, matching Beis Hillel's increasing and Beis Shammai's decreasing lights. Through the Arizal on the eight kings of Edom and the Bnei Yissaschar, he explains that the oil lasted because the 'long days' of Moshiach shone, so all eight lamps stand from the first night. The full lamps are the Jews and the empty ones the nations. A bracha cannot be made over empty vessels, so the menorah must be one piece. On Zos Chanukah, like Shemini Atzeres, all eight are full. He closes with a story about emunah and a brachah.

en: The Rav asks why the Torah repeats the making of the Menorah in Beha'aloscha, mentioning only that it is mikshah, one piece, and why Jews use one menorah of eight lamps instead of separate lamps.
The miracle has two sides, the downfall of the enemies and the salvation of Israel, reflected in the two versions of the brachah and in Beis Shammai's and Beis Hillel's ways of lighting.
The oil burned eight days because the 'long days' of Moshiach shone at that time, so a menorah of eight branches stands even on the first night to show that one day stretched into eight.
The lit lamps represent Klal Yisrael, growing brighter each night, and the dark empty lamps the nations, growing fewer.
The menorah must be one piece because a brachah is not made over empty vessels; as one piece with a lit lamp, its empty lamps are not an empty vessel.
Zos Chanukah is like Shemini Atzeres: all eight lamps are full, none empty, and the light of Moshiach is fully revealed.

title.en: Full lamps and empty lamps

summary.en: The Rav explains that the menorah is made of lit, full lamps and dark, empty ones: the full are Klal Yisrael, growing each night, and the empty are the nations, growing fewer. Like Egypt's darkness while the Jews had light, both are in the menorah. The seven dark lamps correspond to the seven kings of Edom of whom the Torah says 'vayamos'.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and why mikshah

summary.en: The Rav compares Zos Chanukah to Shemini Atzeres, which comes after seven days, when all eight strings of Moshiach's harp play. He then answers why the menorah must be mikshah: a brachah is not made over an empty vessel, and as one piece with a lit lamp the empty lamps are not an empty vessel. The empty lamps are as much a mitzvah as the full ones.

title.en: Tonight all eight lamps are full

summary.en: The Rav says that today, Zos Chanukah, the twenty-fifth of Kislev reaches completion: all eight lamps are full, none empty, and the nations have no part, like Shemini Atzeres. Aharon's avodah gave Jews a menorah holding darkness and light, and 'ken asah' speaks of every Jew's menorah. Tonight all eight lights are holy, a good sign.

title.en: Believing in the light of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav says Jews look at the menorah and believe the light of Moshiach shines from it, and tells of a tzaddik who saw the ushpizin and the Kotzker who answered that believing they come is greater. He closes with a brachah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: מתתיהו בן יוחנן - הכל מתנה וחנינה מה' יתברך. צריכים להללו!

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Matisyahu ben Yochanan's name marks the soul that knows everything it receives is an undeserved gift from Hashem, and that Chanukah, and above all Zos Chanukah, teaches that even nature is a miracle.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Al HaNissim names Matisyahu together with his father, unlike Mordechai on Purim. He brings the Gemara that the world is sustained for the sake of Chanina, and explains that in every generation there is a soul called 'Chanina', who knows nothing is due to him and that all he receives is chesed. Moshe, the humblest of men, and Yaakov, the man of truth, saw themselves this way. Matisyahu ('a gift of Yud-Kei-Vav') ben Yochanan carries the same idea. From the story of Rabbi Chanina's daughter, whose vinegar burned like oil, the Rav explains that for one who sees everything as a gift, nature and miracle are the same. Through Chasam Sofer's picture of the generation that saw manna and then bread from the earth, he teaches that nature is only a veil. Chanukah, the last mitzvah given, seals emunah, and through emunah Mashiach will come.

en: In every generation there is a soul called 'Chanina' who knows that nothing is owed to him and that everything he receives is Hashem's chesed, and the world is sustained for his sake.
The name Matisyahu ben Yochanan expresses this awareness: 'Matisyahu' is a gift of Yud-Kei-Vav, and 'Yochanan' contains 'chanan', grace.
For one who sees everything as a gift, there is no difference between oil burning and vinegar burning: everything is equally a miracle.
Nature is only a veil over G-dliness; a Jew bound to Hashem sees G-dliness in fire, in a tree and in a wall.
The eighth day, Zos Chanukah, taught that even oil burning by nature is a miracle, and that Hashem runs the world.
Chanukah is the last of the mitzvos given, so the count of mitzvos begins with emunah (Anochi) and ends with emunah, and in the merit of emunah Mashiach will come.

title.en: Why Matisyahu is named with his father

summary.en: The Rav asks why Al HaNissim names Matisyahu ben Yochanan with his father's name, while on Purim only Mordechai and Esther are named. He brings the Gemara that the world is sustained for the sake of Chanina, and explains that in every generation there is a soul called 'Chanina' who knows all he receives is Hashem's grace.

title.en: Nothing is due: Moshe, Yaakov and Matisyahu

summary.en: The Rav shows that Moshe Rabbeinu, the humblest of men, davened only for a free gift, and that Yaakov, the man of truth, knew nothing was due to him. He then explains Matisyahu ben Yochanan's name, like Mordechai ben Yair's, as describing the soul: a gift of Yud-Kei-Vav and grace.

title.en: Oil or vinegar: all is a miracle

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one who sees Chanina, Chananiah or Yochanan in a dream will see miracles, and the story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's daughter, whose vinegar burned all Shabbos. He asks how Rabbi Chanina could rely on a miracle, and answers that for one who knows every breath is a gift, oil burning and vinegar burning are the same miracle.

title.en: Manna, bread and the veil of nature

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's picture of the generation born in the desert, who were amazed when bread grew from the earth, and explains that bread from the earth is as wondrous as bread from heaven. He mocks the scientist who thinks 'gravity' explains anything, and teaches that nature is only a veil; one who cleaves to Hashem sees G-dliness in everything, as the Ba'al Shem Tov taught.

title.en: Emunah is planting; the few Chashmonaim

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who dreams of Chanina sees miracles in every bite and breath, and that emunah is 'Zeraim' because a Jew plants knowing that the growth is a miracle, unlike a gentile who is used to it. The Chashmonaim, a handful of people, went to war on the level of Matisyahu ben Yochanan, knowing everything comes from Hashem.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the seal of emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer on the miracle of the first day, and explains that after seven days of miracles the Jews recognized that even the naturally burning oil of the eighth day, Zos Chanukah, was a miracle. Chanukah, the last mitzvah given, closes the mitzvos that began with Anochi, giving the last generation emunah, and in its merit Mashiach will come; he ends with a brachah.

title.en: Stories at the table: sweeping the beis medrash

summary.en: After a long untranscribed gap, stories are told at the table, among them a chassid who swept a beis medrash at night to serve a visiting tzaddik, and Reb Hersh, the attendant of Reb Mendel of Rimanov, whose sweeping cleared away foreign thoughts before davening. Much of the stretch is badly garbled.

catalogTitle: שאתה מדליק ומטיב את הנרות - חנוכה הוא יו"ט של אהרן ומדתו - הוד

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon HaKohen: through the Chanukah lights Aharon's lighting of the Menorah continues in every Jew, bringing his middah of hod, thanksgiving, peace and the hidden light.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Aharon was told his share is greater than the Nesi'im's, since he lights the Menorah, and with the Ramban that this hints at the Chanukah miracle of the Chashmona'im. Building on the Sfas Emes and the Chasam Sofer, he explains that on Chanukah every Jew performs the Temple service and becomes like a kohen. Using the Arizal's teaching that a tzaddik's soul joins whoever does his favorite mitzvah, he explains that Aharon, who never changed in his lighting, is revealed in every Jew who lights. Hoda'ah, he says, is Aharon's middah of hod. He then explains why Zos Chanukah is the final sealing of judgment: the light of Chanukah is the hidden light, and a Jew is judged by the hidden good within him, as the Chozeh of Lublin story shows. He connects shalom bayis, which outweighs the Chanukah light, to Aharon the lover of peace, speaks of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, and closes by urging the year-round thanking of Hashem in the morning davening.

en: The Rav explains, following the Sfas Emes and the Chasam Sofer, that the Chanukah lights are the one remnant of the Temple service left today, so for eight days every Jew becomes like a kohen.
Since Aharon never changed in his lighting, his soul joins every Jew who lights the Chanukah candles with the proper intention, so his lighting lasts forever.
The essence of Chanukah is hallel and hoda'ah, and hoda'ah is the middah of hod, which is Aharon and the Bais HaMikdash.
Zos Chanukah is the final sealing because the Chanukah light is the hidden light, and on it a Jew is judged by the hidden good within him rather than by his deeds.
Shalom bayis outweighs even the Chanukah light because Chanukah is Aharon's Yom Tov, and Aharon loved and pursued peace.
From Chanukah one draws hoda'ah for the whole year: thanking Hashem for His constant supervision and for the daily hidden miracles, above all in the morning davening.

title.en: Untranscribed opening

summary.en: A single long segment of nearly fourteen minutes in which the ASR caught only a few words about the Torah reading of Zos Chanukah; the rest is not transcribed.

title.en: Aharon's share and the Ramban's question

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Aharon's share, lighting the Menorah, is greater than the Nesi'im's, and the Ramban that it hints at the Chanukah miracle; he asks what Chanukah has to do with Aharon and his tribe. He recalls the Sfas Emes and the Chasam Sofer that the Chanukah lights continue the Temple service, so every Jew becomes like a kohen.

title.en: Aharon who never changed lives on in every Jew

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer on 'he did not change': Aharon never skipped the lighting for the ketores. With the Arizal's teaching, illustrated by the story of the Midrash Shmuel and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, that a tzaddik's soul joins one who does his mitzvah, he explains that Aharon's soul joins every Jew who lights Chanukah candles, so his lighting is forever.

title.en: Hallel and hoda'ah: Aharon's middah of hod

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, in Kislev and Teves, stands above the order of months, and that each Jew received a spark of Aharon's soul. Chanukah's essence is hallel and hoda'ah; hoda'ah is hod, which is Aharon and the Bais HaMikdash, and Chanukah trains a Jew to thank Hashem for everything.

title.en: Zos Chanukah as the final sealing; the Lubliner story

summary.en: The Rav cites the Bas Ayin, in the name of the Arizal, that the final sealing is on Zos Chanukah, and asks what this gives a person who did not do real teshuvah. He tells the story, from the Imrei Emes and the Shem MiShmuel, of an informer whose kvittel the Chozeh of Lublin first could not act on because the man's soul was shining while he lit Chanukah candles.

title.en: The hidden light and judgment by inner good

summary.en: The Rav explains the story with the Bnei Yissaschar: the Chanukah light is the hidden light of Moshiach, hidden in every Jew. On Chanukah a Jew is judged by that light rather than by his deeds, as Moshiach will find merit in the worst Jew according to Rabbi Gedalia of Linitz; so even a little teshuvah suffices, which explains the Ruzhiner's saying about Zos Chanukah.

title.en: Shalom bayis outweighs the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Gemara's rule that the Shabbos light comes before the Chanukah light because of shalom bayis is where the Rambam praises peace. He explains it with the Meiri: Shabbos lights are the wife's mitzvah and Chanukah lights the husband's. Chanukah is Aharon's Yom Tov, and Aharon loved and pursued peace, so the greatness of shalom bayis was revealed through the Chanukah light.

title.en: The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy on Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav brings from the Arizal, via the Bnei Yissaschar, that the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy come down over the days of Chanukah and are complete on the eighth day. He connects this to the passuk of the oil running down Aharon's beard, and says each Yom Tov gives a middah for the year: from Chanukah, hod.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for His constant supervision

summary.en: The Rav explains the Modim thanks for 'our lives entrusted in Your hand': Hashem supervises every step Himself. With the Ramban he says one who believes that everything is a miracle thanks Hashem constantly. He urges beginning the day with praise in the morning davening, explaining the passuk of the crucible: praise of Hashem purifies a person and opens the light of Torah. He closes with a tefilah that, on the last day of Chanukah, all should feel the sweetness of praising Hashem and that Chanukah should prepare for the day that is all Shabbos.

catalogTitle: “אנה לידו ושמתי לך מקום” - The Essence of the מצוה of ערי מקלט: Seek Hashem as your Refuge.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Elul is an ir miklat, a city of refuge from the Satan, and that the true refuge in place, time, Torah and soul is always Malchus Shamayim, which Mashiach, whose own mitzvah is the cities of refuge, will complete.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the remez that Elul is a city of refuge, from the passuk 'ina l'yado v'samti lecha makom', and identifies the pursuing avenger with the Satan and the yetzer hara. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that the Satan will err by fleeing to Bozrah instead of Betzer, and asks how such a lamdan could err so plainly. Through the Rambam's three Torah sources for Mashiach, he shows that the unfulfilled mitzvah of adding three cities waits for Mashiach, and proposes that this is Mashiach's own mitzvah. Using the Sefer Yetzirah's place, time and soul, he finds a refuge in each, plus Kriyas Shema in the Torah, all of them Malchus Shamayim. The Satan panics in Betzer because he senses Mashiach there, and flees to Bozrah, the source of Moav's malchus of tumah. The Rav urges running to Torah and teshuvah rather than the protections of the nations, and ends with the 122 days of teshuvah hinted in the sedras.

en: Elul is an ir miklat, hinted in the passuk 'ina l'yado v'samti lecha', and the avenger it protects from is the Satan, the yetzer hara and the Angel of Death.
The Gemara in Makkos says the Satan will err and flee to Bozrah, thinking it is a city of refuge, though the Torah names Betzer.
The mitzvah of adding three more cities of refuge was never fulfilled and waits for Mashiach; the Rav proposes that it is Mashiach's own mitzvah, through which he completes the Torah.
There is a city of refuge in place, in time (Elul through Yom Kippur), in the Torah (Kriyas Shema) and in the soul (Mashiach), and all of them are Malchus Shamayim.
In a time of fear, the Rav says, Jews should run to Torah, mitzvos, teshuvah, bitachon and emunah, and not to the protections of the nations, which are Bozrah.
The teshuvah season stretches from Elul as far as Chanukah, and the 122 pesukim of Ki Savo are a rebuke for last year's unused 122 days.

title.en: Elul as a city of refuge

summary.en: The Rav explains that Elul already begins and shapes the new year, brings the remez of 'Ani l'dodi', and then the remez of 'ina l'yado v'samti lecha', which makes Elul an ir miklat. The avenger who pursues a person is the Satan, the yetzer hara and the Angel of Death.

title.en: Yaakov's flight to Sukkos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that the sequence of Elul, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkos is found in Yaakov's encounter with Esav: the brachos, the gift to Esav's angel, and finally the flight to Sukkos, where he is sheltered by the Shechinah. On Sukkos Jews take refuge under the wings of the Shechinah like a child under its mother's apron.

title.en: The Satan's mistake: Bozrah, not Betzer

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Makkos that at the Geulah the Satan will flee to Bozrah, erring three ways. He focuses on the error of Bozrah: the Satan is a great lamdan who can dress an aveirah as a mitzvah, and every child knows the passuk says Betzer, so why does he run to Bozrah?

title.en: The Rambam: three places that promise Mashiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that three places in the Torah promise Mashiach, the third being the mitzvah to add three cities of refuge, which was never fulfilled. He then lists the Rambam's three simanim of Mashiach, matches them to the three places, and explains through arvus that the whole of Klal Yisrael has fulfilled every mitzvah except this one, which waits for Mashiach.

title.en: Mashiach's own mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the 600,000 root souls correspond to the letters of the Sefer Torah and that every Jew is rooted in one particular mitzvah, as in the Gemara 'with which mitzvah was your father most careful'. He asks what Mashiach's own mitzvah is, and proposes that it is ir miklat, since through it he completes the Torah and is the savior who is Klal Yisrael's refuge.

title.en: A refuge in place, time, Torah and soul

summary.en: From the Sefer Yetzirah's olam, shanah, nefesh, the Rav shows that the ir miklat exists in place (the cities), in Torah (the 6 and 42 words of Shema matching the 48 cities), in time (Elul through Yom Kippur) and in the soul (Mashiach). All of them are kabbalas ol Malchus Shamayim, and he brings the Tzemach Tzedek that a king, and above all Melech HaMashiach, is wholly nullified to Hashem.

title.en: Moshe begins, Mashiach completes

summary.en: The Rav explains that the king's fear of Heaven spreads to the people, that Moshe was the first king and first redeemer and Mashiach the last, sharing one soul. Moshe designated the first cities of refuge and Mashiach will add the last three; he shows by gematria that both phrases equal 'som tasim alecha melech'.

title.en: Why the Satan flees Betzer for Bozrah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the shofar confuses the Satan because it reminds him of the shofar of Mashiach. Returning to the opening question, he explains that in Betzer the Satan senses Mashiach, for Betzer in the Zohar's ribua gematria equals David ben Yishai, panics, and argues that Bozrah is Betzer's feminine form, since in tumah the feminine dominates, as the Ohr HaChaim describes. But Bozrah is exactly where Hashem will slaughter the Satan.

title.en: Moav exports malchus

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shem MiShmuel quoting his father-in-law, the Kotzker, that malchus is foreign to Yisrael and was imported from Moav through Rus. Rashi explains that Bozrah, a city of Moav, gave Edom its king, Yovav ben Zerach, so the Satan flees from the malchus of kedushah in Betzer to the malchus of tumah in Bozrah, which Mashiach will destroy.

title.en: Run to Torah, not to Bozrah

summary.en: The Rav describes the fear in the world and in Eretz Yisrael today, and says those who lack emunah run to Bozrah. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that the Torah is a city of refuge, and recalls how gedolim, among them Rav Chaim Kanievsky, kept learning during the missile attacks instead of running to sealed rooms; the true refuge is Torah, mitzvos, teshuvah and emunah.

title.en: 30, 40, 52 and 122 days of teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that tzaddikim need only the 30 days of Elul, beinonim need 40, and that the Zohar and the Arizal extend teshuvah to Shemini Atzeres and even the last day of Chanukah. He shows that the sedras read now have matching numbers of pesukim: Vayelech 30, Nitzavim 40, Haazinu 52, and together 122, the days until Chanukah, and notes his son-in-law's remark that Ki Savo also has 122.

title.en: Ki Savo: last year's 122 days

summary.en: The Rav answers that Ki Savo's 122 pesukim, read so the year ends with its curses, point to last year's 122 days of teshuvah and the tragedies that followed, as a rebuke not to repeat the mistake. He calls on everyone to use Elul and Tishrei, run to the refuge under the Shechinah's apron, and closes with brachos for a good year and the coming of Mashiach.

catalogTitle: יום שמיני של חנוכה מורה על אחדות ישראל

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, gathers all of Chanukah and all of Klal Yisrael into one, like the thirty-six lights that merge into a single flame, and reveals the hidden light in every Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that a gathering of Jews in love repairs the sale of Yosef, and that Chanukah is the aspect of Yosef. In the days of the Nesi'im each tribe had its own day, but Zos Chanukah counts everything together. Every Jew is a letter of the Torah and holds one mitzvah; the thirty-six lights match thirty-six masechtos, and on Zos Chanukah the leftover wicks are burned in one flame. This unity undoes the Greeks, and it rests on bittul before every other Jew. Bending down to light the menorah brings down the thirteen middos of rachamim and the treasure of free gifts. Chanukah comes from the fiftieth gate, the Yovel, like the Exodus; the menorah is a model of the third Beis HaMikdash. The last light is the light of Moshiach. The empty cups of the menorah stand for Jews whose hidden light is not yet lit, and the Rav closes that on Zos Chanukah every simple Jew can achieve what tzaddikim achieve on Yom Kippur.

en: Jews sitting together with love is the repair of the sale of Yosef, and Chanukah is the aspect of Yosef.
In the twelve days of the Nesi'im each tribe had its own festival, but on Zos Chanukah everything is counted together as one.
The thirty-six lights correspond to the thirty-six masechtos, and on Zos Chanukah all the wicks are burned together in one great flame.
The heart of Yiddishkeit is to be mevatel oneself before every Jew, because each one has a virtue that one does not have.
Bending down to light the Chanukah lights accustoms a Jew to humility, which brings down the thirteen middos of rachamim and the treasure of free gifts.
The menorah, made by Hashem Himself, is a model of the third Beis HaMikdash and of the fiftieth gate.
The empty cups of a one-piece menorah stand for Jews whose hidden light does not yet shine; Hashem judges them by that hidden light.

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew holds one mitzvah, that the thirty-six lights match thirty-six masechtos, and that on Zos Chanukah the wicks are burned together in one flame. This unity undoes the Greeks; it rests on bittul before every Jew, and he brings the Divrei Yisrael on Yosef's words to his brothers about different paths.

title.en: Bending down and the treasure of free gifts

summary.en: The Rav explains that lighting below ten tefachim trains a Jew to bend down, which is why Al HaNissim is in Modim and why Chanukah brings down the thirteen middos of rachamim. He brings the Midrash of the treasure of free gifts, Yishmael's teshuvah in letting Yitzchak go first, and ties this to Yosef and to the Yovel.

title.en: Mai Chanukah: the light of the Yovel

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Gemara asks 'What is Chanukah?' and answers that Chanukah comes from the fiftieth gate, the Yovel, like the Exodus, which is awakened by questions. The Yovel comes from Hashem alone, not from a person's deeds, so even the lowest Jew will run to Moshiach, and the third Beis HaMikdash will be built by Hashem.

title.en: The menorah and the third Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Rav explains why Moshe found the menorah hard: it was made by Hashem Himself and is a model of the third Beis HaMikdash and of the fiftieth gate, which Moshe did not attain. On Zos Chanukah the last light, matching the last masechta, completes the light of Moshiach and the rebuilding of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Chanukah completes the crown

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the Hallel still to be said and explains that Chanukah, the last mitzvah instituted by the Sages, completes the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, the crown that will be placed on Moshiach. He ties Chanukah to chen, to Yosef's blessing to Binyamin and to Kislev, and says Chanukah's judgment is by the hidden light in every Jew.

title.en: The empty cups of the menorah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the custom is a one-piece menorah with empty cups, when one makes no brachah over empty vessels. He answers that the empty cups are Jews whose hidden light does not yet shine; Hashem sees that they are not empty, and when Moshiach comes all the lights will shine toward the menorah.

title.en: Every simple Jew a tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav repeats the saying of the Ruzhiner that what tzaddikim achieve on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur every simple Jew can achieve on Zos Chanukah, and explains it with 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim'. He says every minute of Zos Chanukah is a treasure, and closes with brachos for children, life and sustenance and for the revelation of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: סעודת רשות - היחיד או הרבים? ואודות פרות השמנות הנבלעות בתוך פרות הכחושות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah meal is a 'seudas reshus' in which singing turns the public domain of golus into a private domain of Hashem, and that the lean cows of Pharaoh's dream, which swallowed the fat ones, will in the end have to spit out every holy spark.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that Chanukah carries no obligation of a meal, so its meal is a 'seudas reshus'. Chanukah lights are placed in the public domain below ten tefachim, bringing a private domain of holiness into the public one. 'Reshus' alone lacks a word; by singing praise, as one must at a redemption, a Jew adds 'hayachid', because even in the public domain there is a spark of G-dliness. In Pharaoh's dream, the lean cows stood beside the fat ones, stunned like a person entering Jerusalem, because the sitra achra knows the power of holiness and that it must eventually spit out what it swallowed. From the Midrash on 'ketz sam lachoshech' and Yosef's two extra years in prison he explains how a set time of redemption can be prolonged, calls on each Jew to hasten it, and sees baalei teshuvah as the first drops before the rain.

en: Since Chanukah has no obligatory meal, its meal is a 'seudas reshus', and by singing at it a Jew adds the missing word and makes it a 'reshus hayachid'.
The Chanukah light is placed in the public domain below ten tefachim, bringing a private domain of holiness into the public one.
The lean cows that swallowed the fat ones represent the sitra achra swallowing Jewish souls, but in the end it must spit out everything.
A set time of redemption can be prolonged, as Yosef's release was delayed two years, and each Jew should ask what he does to hasten it.
The teshuvah movement before Moshiach is like the light rain that comes before a heavy rain.

title.en: Seudas reshus: adding the missing word

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Chanukah with Purim, which has an obligatory meal, and explains the Chanukah meal as a 'seudas reshus'. The light is placed in the public domain, and by singing, as one must at a redemption, a Jew reveals the spark of G-dliness there and makes it a 'reshus hayachid'.

title.en: Why the lean cows stood still

summary.en: The Rav asks why the hungry lean cows of Pharaoh's dream 'stood' beside the fat ones. Comparing them to a person who stops in awe on entering Jerusalem, he explains that the sitra achra knows the power of holiness and that whatever it swallows it must in the end spit out, and more.

title.en: A ketz that was prolonged

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on 'ketz sam lachoshech' and a calculation of the ketz attributed to the Arizal that passed without redemption. He answers from Yosef, who was meant to be in prison ten years but had it extended because he leaned on the butler instead of on Hashem alone.

title.en: Chanukah, time to hasten the ketz

summary.en: The Rav calls Chanukah a time of redemption when the hidden light is revealed, and says each Jew should make a reckoning of what he does so the ketz is hastened. From the public domain of golus one makes a private domain by singing zemiros before the redemption, and he closes with a tefilah that Hashem's kingship be revealed.

title.en: Niggun

summary.en: The Rav returns to the swallowed souls, so hidden they cannot be recognized as Jews, and brings the Gemara that light rain precedes a heavy rain: before Moshiach there are already glimmers of teshuvah. He describes young men he saw who became chassidish and daven with fire, and says that one must keep kindling more lights.

catalogTitle: The Great Effect of Tekias Shofar. The נסיון of עקידת יצחק as Applicable to our Generation

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Akeidah was a test of serving Hashem while He seems far away and full of contradictions, that our generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha lives through that same test, and that the shofar we received from the Akeidah disperses the clouds and renews the world.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Zohar's picture of the end of the year: the bounty allotted last Rosh Hashanah is used up, and clouds separate Hashem from Knesses Yisrael. Our earthly shofar arouses the heavenly shofar, disperses the clouds and draws down new bounty, and with the hundred sounds and the verses of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros Klal Yisrael recreates the world with the Ten Utterances. To explain this he turns to the Akeidah. Nisayon also means raising up. Why was the Akeidah, a direct command from Hashem, the hardest test? The Zohar answers that Avraham saw Hashem from afar: the command contradicted the promise about Yitzchak, and he obeyed without understanding. Following the Ramban that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the Rav teaches that the last generation before Mashiach, the heel of Adam's body, faces this same test of confusion. Avraham's emunah reaching down to the heel gives us the strength to hold on, and the ram of the Akeidah gave us the shofar.

en: At the end of the year the bounty is used up and clouds separate Hashem from Klal Yisrael; the shofar disperses them and draws down new bounty for the coming year.
Through the shofar and the ten verses of each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, Klal Yisrael recreates the world with the Ten Utterances.
The test of the Akeidah was that Hashem's command contradicted His promise about Yitzchak, and Avraham obeyed while confused and without understanding.
Since the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha must pass the test of the Akeidah: emunah amid questions and hester panim.
Avraham's emunah reached down to the heel, and that gives his children the strength to keep emunah in the hardest conditions; emunah will never leave Klal Yisrael.
The shofar of Rosh Hashanah comes from the ram of the Akeidah, and it renews both the calendar year and, at the end of days, the whole world.
Even when Hashem seems distant, His love for Klal Yisrael is not extinguished; He loves them even more because He sees their struggle.

title.en: The shofar disperses the year-end clouds

summary.en: Following the Zohar, the Rav describes how the bounty of the past year runs out and clouds come between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. The earthly shofar arouses the heavenly shofar, disperses the clouds and brings new bounty, and with the hundred sounds and the verses of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros Klal Yisrael recreates the world with the Ten Utterances.

title.en: Nisayon as raising up; the first test and the last

summary.en: The Rav turns to the Akeidah, explains that nisayon also means raising up, like a child promoted after a test, and describes Avraham's first test in Ur Kasdim, where he gave his life for a G-d who had never spoken to him. He asks why the Akeidah, commanded by Hashem Himself, should be harder.

title.en: He saw the Makom from afar

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar on 'he saw the place from afar': Avraham saw Hashem as distant, because the command to bring Yitzchak contradicted the promise that his offspring would come through Yitzchak, and Hashem does not change His mind. Avraham refused to dwell on the question and obeyed blindly.

title.en: Why Avraham could not see the answer

summary.en: Through Rashi, the Rav shows that the answer was simple: Hashem had said to bring Yitzchak up, not to slaughter him. Avraham did not see it because a test means the answers are hidden; this is hester panim, which can come on a person or a generation, and Avraham told the Satan he would not listen to him.

title.en: The deeds of the Avos as a sign for the children

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban's rule that whatever happened to the Avos foreshadows their children, illustrated by Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim. It follows that Klal Yisrael must pass ten tests, and the last one, before Mashiach, is the Akeidah's test of a clouded mind and a heart without feeling.

title.en: Malachi: believers in the last generation

summary.en: The Rav explains that Malachi, the last prophet, describes the generation before Mashiach saying that serving Hashem does not pay, yet promises that those who fear Hashem will gather and strengthen one another. As Avraham held on to emunah, a backbone of believers will remain, and the Medrash says they will rejoice more over keeping their emunah than over the Geulah itself.

title.en: Our questions and the heel of Adam

summary.en: The Rav says our generation is full of questions on Hashem, which are easy to answer only after the test. Every generation corresponds to a limb of Adam's body, and the last generation is the heel, which has no feeling. At the Akeidah Avraham was transported into this condition, and Hashem's blessing 'eikev asher shamata' alludes to it.

title.en: The Akeidah fulfilled the promise

summary.en: Bringing the Zohar, the Rav explains that Yitzchak could not have children before the Akeidah; there his neshamah left him and returned with an addition, so that right afterward Rivkah's birth is told. The Akeidah, which seemed to cancel the promise, actually fulfilled it, and what seems bad to a person with emunah turns out to be for his good.

title.en: Emes, the last word of Shema

summary.en: The Rav says that today Hashem is distant and this is our tafkid in a world of kefirah. The 248 words of Shema correspond to the 248 limbs; the first word is the head and the last, emes, is the heel, and in ikvesa d'Meshicha the Gemara says emes will be missing, so one must believe in it in the dark.

title.en: Chavakuk's one mitzvah: emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that later generations concentrated the 613 mitzvos, until Chavakuk stood the whole Torah on emunah, because small generations cannot put full effort into every mitzvah. Pure emunah is hard today, but because Avraham's emunah reached the heel, emunah is eternal in Klal Yisrael and gives us strength now.

title.en: Mashiach girded with tzedakah and emunah

summary.en: The Rav describes Mashiach pleading to come while the Satan accuses, and says he will prevail with the strength of tzedakah and emunah, which are inseparable, as the passuk in Yeshayah calls them the belt of his loins. He urges strengthening emunah and learning sefarim that strengthen it.

title.en: The ram of the Akeidah and Shema Yisrael

summary.en: Returning to the opening, the Rav explains that at the Akeidah Avraham dispersed the clouds of confusion and his emunah was renewed, and from the ram caught by its horns we received the shofar, which renews the world each year. Rosh Hashanah is the head of the year as emunah is the head of the mitzvos; Shema Yisrael, the last verse of Malchiyos, equals 'shofar shel ayil' in gematria, and the Gemara says the kingship is accepted through the shofar.

title.en: The year as a miniature of world history

summary.en: The Rav explains that the year is a miniature of the world's whole history, which ends at the end of days and begins again. Bereishis hints at 'bara tayish', the ram created at the beginning for Avraham, so the world begins with the strength of the shofar, and the new world will also begin with the great shofar. Today the universal year is at its end, covered with thick clouds.

title.en: Birth pangs of Mashiach and Hashem's love

summary.en: The Rav compares our time to the seventy sighs of a woman in labor, matching the seventy words of Lamnatzeach that end with 'b'yom kareinu', where we stand now. Malachi opens with 'I have loved you', and the haftarah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah says Hashem appears from afar with eternal love; the hardship is for our good like the Akeidah. He closes with a brachah for teshuvah sheleimah and the great shofar.

catalogTitle: בזאת חנוכה נעשה הדלקה אחת מכל הנרות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that on Zos Chanukah all the lights, all the masechtos, all the shevatim and all of Klal Yisroel come together into one great lighting, through which every Jew can reach what a tzaddik reaches on Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara's 'pach shel shemen': the jar was nearly empty, yet its last drops burned all eight nights. He brings the Ruzhiner: what a tzaddik achieves on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew achieves on Zos Chanukah, and contrasts the wordless shofar with Chanukah's hallel and thanks. Chanukah is the last mitzvah, completing the crown of mitzvos; its lights match the masechtos, ending with Niddah, galus and Eliyahu. The seudah is a voluntary mitzvah of love that unites Jews, and on Zos Chanukah, like the total of the nesi'im's offerings, everything joins into one. Through the Ramban, the Sfas Emes and a story of Rav Chaim Vital, he shows that Aharon lights with every Jew. He adds that Zos Chanukah is a day of remembering the barren, tells of a ba'al teshuvah's lineage, and closes with the Ruzhiner's word about winning.

en: The Ruzhiner said that what a tzaddik can accomplish on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew can accomplish on Zos Chanukah, because Chanukah reaches down to the lowest levels.
On Rosh Hashanah Hashem is served with the wordless breath of the shofar; on Chanukah, when there is already speech, He is served with hallel and thanks.
Chanukah is the last mitzvah given, and with it the crown of the mitzvos is completed.
The Chanukah lights correspond to the masechtos of the Oral Torah; the last, Niddah, matches the final galus and ends with Eliyahu, herald of Moshiach.
On Zos Chanukah all the masechtos, all the shevatim and all the lights join into one, as the Torah totals all the nesi'im's offerings together.
Since the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Menorah, every Jew's home becomes a Beis HaMikdash and Aharon HaKohen comes to light together with him.

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Rosh Hashanah, served with the wordless shofar, with Chanukah, served with hallel and thanks. Chanukah is the last mitzvah that completes the crown of mitzvos, and through the Bnei Yissaschar in the name of Rav Pinchas of Koretz its lights match the masechtos, ending with Niddah, galus and Eliyahu.

title.en: A seudah of love that unites

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah seudah is voluntary, a mitzvah Jews take on out of love, like hiddur, and that such a meal brings Jews together. Each Jew has his own light and masechta, and on Zos Chanukah all are thrown into one great fire of achdus.

title.en: Zos Chanukah: everything joins into one

summary.en: Each day of Chanukah is the yom tov of one nasi, but Zos Chanukah belongs to all, as the Torah totals all the offerings. The Rav adds the thirteen middos of rachamim and the Arizal's teaching that each day's mitzvos rise the next morning, tells how the Imrei Emes was aroused by 'kol hakelim', and invites all to daven together with all their kelim.

title.en: Aharon lights with every Jew

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that Aharon's consolation hints to the Chanukah lights, and asks what aliyah this is for his tribe if all Jews light. Through the Sfas Emes, that Chanukah is a remembrance of the Menorah, and Rav Chaim Vital's story of Rav Pinchas ben Yair, he explains that Aharon HaKohen enters every Jew who lights.

title.en: The hidden Menorah and remembering the barren

summary.en: The Rav adds the reverse: through the Chiddushei HaRim, quoted by the Sfas Emes, that the hidden Menorah still burns, our lighting kindles Aharon's Menorah. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah, and above all Zos Chanukah, is a time of remembering the barren, and says to pray for Tzion.

title.en: A ba'al teshuvah and his lineage; blessings

summary.en: The Rav tells of a ba'al teshuvah whose mother traced her lineage and found she descends from Rav Meir of Premishlan, and explains that Chanukah lights are lit outside, to kindle extinguished souls. He ends with blessings and with the eight names of Moshiach in Yeshayahu, which he links to the eight days.

title.en: What is won on Zos Chanukah stays won

summary.en: After a long stretch the transcript barely records (likely singing at the seudah), the Rav quotes the Ruzhiner that what is won on Zos Chanukah is not lost, tells of the custom of tzaddikim to drink punch on Zos Chanukah, and closes wishing that Chanukah flow into Purim in Yerushalayim with Moshiach.

catalogTitle: בחינת שמיני עצרת' הקב"ה רוצה להיות אצלינו עוד יום אחד

oneLiner.en: The Rav contrasts Shemini Atzeres, when Jews come up to Hashem and He holds them back one more day, with Zos Chanukah, when Hashem Himself comes down to the lowest Jews to stay with them and light them up.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shemini Atzeres: Sukkos has a reason, but Shemini Atzeres has none except that Hashem wants to be with His children, as a father needs no reason to come to his child's simcha. Chanukah goes further. On Shemini Atzeres the Jews come up to Hashem; on Chanukah Hashem comes down to the extinguished souls in the street, and on Zos Chanukah He says He will stay below with them, like a king who comes to a lowly place because his bride is there. From this the Rav speaks of drawing close the distant Jews. He brings the Targum Yonasan that the korbanos of the twelve nesiim, read on Zos Chanukah, nullify the twelve princes of Yishmael, and tells how Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky explained why religious children honor their parents. He closes that Zos Chanukah sums up all of Chanukah, nullifying Esav and Yishmael, and blesses the listeners with a good year.

en: Shemini Atzeres has no reason of its own; Hashem simply wants to be together with the Jews, as a father comes to his child's simcha without needing a reason.
On Shemini Atzeres the Jews come up to Hashem, while on Chanukah Hashem comes down to the lowest levels, to the extinguished souls in the street, to light them up.
Zos Chanukah is a day for drawing close distant Jews who do not even know Shema Yisroel, and for letting oneself be drawn close.
Following the Targum Yonasan, the korbanos of the twelve nesiim nullify the twelve princes of Yishmael.
Zos Chanukah is the sum of all the days of Chanukah, when one takes stock of what one gained, and it is even greater than Chanukah itself.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that on Zos Chanukah the small, hidden point of holiness in every Jew, the 'pach shemen' that was never defiled, prevails over the great mass of bad, as the few prevailed over the many.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Yehuda repeats to Yosef everything both already knew, and answers that he wanted to settle it in his own mind and accept Hashem's guidance in every detail. Every event holds the hidden light of Hashem's will, but the klipah of Yavan covers it; the Chanukah lights reveal it, just as the two words 'Ani Yosef' answered all the brothers' suffering. He brings the Sfas Emes that in these days one must strengthen the small point found in every Jew, the pure flask that keeps its blessing. Chanukah comes from the 'eighth world' above nature, so its miracle followed no rules: the few overcame the many. Zos Chanukah is therefore the final sealing for those whose sins outweigh their merits. He ties this to the ner maaravi, a Ruzhiner story about plain Jews, the Kosel, and 'lo me'astim'.

en: Yehuda repeated what was already known in order to settle it in his own mind and accept Hashem's guidance in every detail.
Hashem's will is hidden in every event as the 'ohr haganuz'; the klipah of Yavan covers it and lighting the Chanukah candles reveals it.
Every Jew has a small point, like the pure flask of oil, which nothing can extinguish and on which blessing rests.
Chanukah comes from the 'eighth world' above nature, so its miracle followed no rules of nature or arithmetic: the few held the many.
Zos Chanukah is the final sealing for those who could not be judged favorably by the count on Rosh Hashanah, because then a small point of mitzvos outweighs many sins.
The ner maaravi and the Kosel Hamaaravi represent the point that is never extinguished, the worth of the plain Jews who sit by the western wall.

title.en: Why Yehuda repeated everything

summary.en: After an opening niggun, the Rav asks why Yehuda retells Yosef all that happened, and answers that he wanted it settled in his mind so as to accept Hashem's guidance in every detail. Nothing happens by chance, but the klipah of Yavan covers this point.

title.en: The hidden light and 'Ani Yosef'

summary.en: The Rav explains that the hidden light of Hashem's will is in every event, and the Chanukah lights reveal it. In the parsha things only get worse for the brothers until two words, 'Ani Yosef', answer everything, as the Midrash says all will be answered when Hashem says 'Ani Hashem'.

title.en: The small point and the eighth world

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes that in these days one must strengthen the small point in every Jew, the pure flask that keeps its blessing. Chanukah, from the 'eighth world' above nature, let one night's oil burn eight nights, and like a bris on the eighth day the Jew laughs at nature.

title.en: The few held the many

summary.en: Citing the Maharal, the Rav explains the Chanukah miracle as 'a little holding much', like the Beis Hamikdash courtyard and the victory of the few over the many. In this world bad is the majority, yet Zos Chanukah, with all eight days' wicks burnt together, shows the good prevailing.

title.en: Zos Chanukah as the final sealing

summary.en: The Rav returns to the Sfas Emes on the small point and asks what Zos Chanukah's final sealing adds to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Rosh Hashanah judges by count, merits against sins; Zos Chanukah is for those whose sins are many, when a small point of mitzvos outweighs them, as will be revealed in the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Taking Chanukah along; Selach na

summary.en: The Rav links the hidden light to chein and to Aharon, and says one must take the warmth of Chanukah along afterward. He brings the Likutei Moharan that 'selach na' holds the initials of Chanukah, explains why the words about sin are left out, and connects Mattisyahu ben Yochanan to Rosh Hashanah and to grace.

title.en: The ner maaravi and the plain Jews

summary.en: The Rav connects the Chanukah miracle to the ner maaravi of Shimon HaTzaddik, a testimony that the Shechinah rests in Israel. He tells how the Ruzhiner refused to come to a shul that would keep out the plain Jews, and explains that the western wall, where plain Jews sit, holds the point that is never extinguished, like the Kosel Hamaaravi.

title.en: 'Lo me'astim' and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's reading of 'lo me'astim' as referring to the days of the Greeks, and says that 'lo me'astim' equals the ner maaravi in gematria. He says a Jew should leave Chanukah taking the hidden light along, and closes with a blessing for a good final sealing; garbled table talk and untranscribed audio follow.

catalogTitle: Recreating the World through מלכיות זכרונות שופרות; תקיעת שופר

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every Rosh Hashanah the creation of Adam and the world is truly repeated, and that through the shofar and the pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros each Jew returns to his pure root and becomes a partner in re-creating the world.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk that Hashem blew the breath of life into Adam: blowing comes from a person's very insides, more than speech. Since shanah means repetition, he compares the year to a rotary file: when Rosh Hashanah comes around, Adam is created anew, and with the shofar we blow that breath back to Hashem. As at the first creation, angels argue each year whether man should be re-created. But every Jew has a hidden point that wants Hashem's will, as the Rambam explains about one who is coerced until he says he wants. This point is the level of Bereishis, the first of the ten utterances, which is above speech; from it comes the atonement of Yom Kippur, and the shofar speaks to Hashem from there without words. Hashem makes each Jew a partner in re-creating his part of the world through the ten pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros. Finally, the shofar is the sound of return, like the Yovel.

en: Hashem blew the breath of life into Adam, and blowing comes from a person's innermost being, deeper than speech.
Shanah means repetition, so each Rosh Hashanah the creation of Adam truly happens again, not just as a remembrance.
In the depth of his heart every Jew, even a rasha, wants to do Hashem's will; this point is beyond words and beyond the angels' grasp.
The shofar speaks to Hashem from the level that precedes speech, the level of Bereishis, where no sin reaches.
On Rosh Hashanah Hashem gives every Jew the task of re-creating the world, through the ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros.
Rosh Hashanah is a return to the root, like the Yovel, and the shofar is the sound of that return.

title.en: The breath of life blown back each year

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'vayipach' means Hashem blew the soul into Adam from His innermost. Since shanah means repetition, he pictures the year as a rotary file of days, so that each Rosh Hashanah Adam is truly created anew, and with the shofar we blow that breath back to Hashem.

title.en: The angels debate man's creation every year

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Hashem consulted the angels before creating Adam, some for and some against, and those against were cast down to this world. Since the year repeats, every Rosh Hashanah angels again argue whether each person deserves another year.

title.en: The hidden point that wants Hashem's will

summary.en: The Rav explains that the angels cannot grasp the Jewish neshamah: in every Jew is a hidden point, beyond words, that does not want to sin. He brings the Gemara that one who refuses to bring a korban is coerced until he says 'I want', and the Rambam's explanation that the coercion only subdues the body and the yetzer hara so the real inner will comes out.

title.en: Bereishis, the tenth level above speech

summary.en: The Rav describes ten levels of holiness up to the Kodesh HaKodashim, where the Kohen Gadol gains atonement on Yom Kippur. He brings the Gemara that 'Bereishis' is also one of the ten utterances, and the Maggid of Mezritch's explanation that it is above speech; there every Jew's pure neshamah wants no sin, and from there comes Yom Kippur's atonement.

title.en: The shofar: speaking without words

summary.en: The Rav explains that the shofar speaks to Hashem from the inner breath before it is formed into words, the level where no sin reaches, and that this inner will declared on Rosh Hashanah is revealed on Yom Kippur. He then explains why the makri does not announce the very first tekiah: not because of a hefsek, but because words are not yet created.

title.en: Re-creating the world with ten pesukim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem tells every Jew to create the world anew on Rosh Hashanah through teshuvah and tefillah, with ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros paralleling the ten utterances, and a hundred sounds. As 'na'aseh adam' shows, man is a partner, and like the generation of the Mabul each person's deeds shape his part of the world; he urges saying the pesukim with full kavanah.

title.en: Shofar and Yovel: returning to the root

summary.en: The Rav explains the law of return: in the Yovel, the fiftieth year, everyone goes back to his land, and the fiftieth day after Pesach was Matan Torah with the shofar. From the burning of the Beis HaMikdash on the tenth of Av until Rosh Hashanah is fifty days, so the shofar of Rosh Hashanah is the sound of returning to Hashem. He closes with wishes for a good Rosh Hashanah.

catalogTitle: ע"י שירות ותשבחות זוכים לאור של חנוכה

oneLiner.en: Through the Chiddushei HaRim, the Rav explains that the light of Chanukah is Aharon's own light still burning, that it demands more than a person's strength, that Hallel and songs of praise make Chanukah a Yom Tov, and that this light must reach those who are far away.

abstract.en: The Rav repeats teachings of the Chiddushei HaRim on Chanukah. Rashi says Aharon was consoled for missing the dedication of the Mishkan with the lighting of the menorah, and the Ramban, puzzled, links it to the Chanukah of the Chashmonaim. The Chiddushei HaRim explains that Aharon's ner hama'aravi was never extinguished and still burns in its hiding place, and the Chanukah lights come from it; this is 'Zos Chanukah'. The mitzvah of Chanukah also demands more than a person's strength, beyond 'with all your means', since the miracle came through mesirus nefesh. The poskim say singing praises turns the Chanukah meal into a seudas mitzvah: the Gemara says the days were fixed as Yom Tov with Hallel and thanksgiving, so the praise itself makes the day a Yom Tov. Finally, Chanukah light must reach those far away, and the Rav calls for supporting kiruv as an opportunity Hashem sends today.

Other Yamim Tovim bring down the lights of their miracles, but on Chanukah the very same miracle still burns, even physically.
The mitzvah of Chanukah demands more than a person's strength, beyond 'with all your means', since the miracle came through mesirus nefesh.
Saying Hallel and singing praises is what turns Chanukah into a Yom Tov, and so it makes the meal a seudas mitzvah.
The Chanukah light must be brought to those who are 'below ten tefachim', the ones far from Torah.
The unprecedented opportunity for kiruv in this generation is a sign that Hashem is sending the merit of the mitzvah before the ingathering of the exiles.

Milah and priah form the same pair. Gehinnom has a fire for sins and snow for mitzvos done coldly, and the eight Chanukah lights, above nature, are the fire of zerizus that answers the snow. Like Shemini Atzeres for Sukkos, the eighth day of Chanukah is above time and carries the fire of Chanukah into the whole year.
What stays fixed after Chanukah is Hallel and hoda'ah, and they should continue all year with fire.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Rosh Hashanah is at heart the coronation of Hashem as King, and that the judgment of the day follows from Hashem creating a new and better world each year, in which a person must earn a place by improving.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the principle that whatever happened in the Torah repeats itself every year, so on Rosh Hashanah Hashem re-creates the world, the ten days of teshuvah matching the ten utterances of creation. He notes that the Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur brachos speak only of Malchus, Hashem's kingship, and hardly mention judgment. Citing his Rebbe, he explains that the judgment is a byproduct of the coronation: re-creating His world, Hashem decides who fits its purpose. Drawing on the Tanya, he adds that each year's world is higher than the last, so being as good as last year is not enough; one must improve. Shabbos Shuvah makes every Jew a partner in the new creation, and Yom Kippur, the tenth day, is the Kodesh HaKodashim of the calendar, when each Jew should reach the inner point of his heart that wants only Hashem's will.

en: Every event in the Torah repeats itself each year, so on Rosh Hashanah and in the ten days that follow Hashem creates the world anew.
The brachos of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are about Malchus, the coronation of Hashem, and do not speak of the day as a day of judgment.
The judgment is a byproduct of the coronation: as Hashem makes His new world, He decides who will serve its purpose and who would spoil it.
Each year's world is higher than the last, so being as good as last year is not enough; a person must improve to fit into the new year.
Through keeping Shabbos Shuvah properly a Jew becomes Hashem's partner in creating the new year.
Yom Kippur is the Kodesh HaKodashim in time, and on it every Jew should reach the inner chamber of his heart that wants only to do Hashem's will.
