title.en: Creation repeats every Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav explains that events in the Torah are not commemorations but repeat every year, like the geulah of Nisan and Kabbalas HaTorah on Shavuos. So the creation of the world repeats each Rosh Hashanah, with each of the ten days matching one of the ten utterances, which is why a year is called shanah, a repetition.

title.en: Malchus, and why it is a day of judgment

summary.en: The Rav shows that the Shemoneh Esrei of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is entirely about Malchus, Hashem's coronation, and that the mention of judgment in Zichronos is not the core of the day. He brings his Rebbe's explanation: since Hashem re-creates the world, He decides who fits its purpose and who would spoil it, so the judgment is a byproduct of the coronation day, while the day itself is one of joy.

title.en: Each year a better world

summary.en: Adding to his Rebbe's words, the Rav says Hashem does not duplicate last year's world but creates a better one, even if the streets and the shuls seem to show decline. He brings the sefarim that the world improves with each generation, and Rebbe Reb Bunim's teaching that although earlier souls were greater, the innermost point of the heart becomes better in every generation.

title.en: Last year's mark is not enough

summary.en: The Rav reads from the Tanya that each Rosh Hashanah the light of the past year withdraws and a new, higher light comes down. From this he concludes that a person who is merely no worse than last year is failing the test, since he must be promoted into a better world, and he brings the piyut's call to improve one's deeds as the heavens themselves are improved.

title.en: Shabbos Shuvah: partner in the new creation

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, and especially on Shabbos Shuvah, Hashem takes each Jew as a partner in creating the new year, since keeping Shabbos is testimony to creation. He urges a Shabbos like never before, with a cheshbon hanefesh, care in its laws, Torah and davening, and joy, and brings the Shelah and the passuk in Tehillim that one should give Hashem pleasure and nachas.

title.en: Yom Kippur, the Kodesh HaKodashim of the heart

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yom Kippur is the tenth day, parallel to the tenth utterance and the tenth level of holiness, the Kodesh HaKodashim, and that each Jew who does teshuvah enters it with the Kohen Gadol in his soul. Every Jew carries an inner chamber in his heart that wants only Hashem's will, as the Rambam explains, and on Yom Kippur he should dig to reach it. He closes noting the days left until Yom Kippur and asking to daven for Klal Yisrael.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, which opens the dark month of Teves, shows Jews Hashem's love, just as Hashem spoke to Yaakov with love 'in the visions of the night' as he went down to Mitzrayim, and that this light must be taken along into Teves.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the sefarim's teaching that Teves is a hard month, the time of the longest night, of darkness and hester panim, and that Chanukah stands at its head to crush the head of the wicked and sweeten the judgments so that Jews can pass through it. He connects this to Parshas Vayigash: Yaakov, about to go down to the exile of Mitzrayim, the darkness of place as Teves is the darkness of time, is told by Hashem 'in the visions of the night' not to fear, for Hashem goes down with him. Chanukah, which the Rambam calls a beloved mitzvah, is a sign of Hashem's love, like the double 'Yaakov, Yaakov' and 'Avraham, Avraham' at the akeidah. A Jew must carry this love and light into Teves, strengthen himself in Torah and tefillah, use the last hours of Zos Chanukah with simple emunah, as the Ruzhiner taught, and bring the Gemara, siddur and Tehillim with him through the dark period until Moshiach.

en: Teves is a hard month of long nights and hester panim, and Chanukah at its head cuts off the head of its darkness and sweetens the judgments so Jews can pass through it.
Mitzrayim is the darkness of place as Teves is the darkness of time, and Yaakov going down there was told by Hashem 'in the visions of the night' not to fear.
Chanukah is a beloved mitzvah through which Hashem shows the Jews that He loves them.
A Jew must take the light and love of Chanukah with him into Teves and strengthen himself in Torah and tefillah.
The light of Zos Chanukah is the greatest light, the eight that is above nature, and it leads into the heart of Teves.
Teves is a time ruled by the 'dogs', and one passes through it by taking along the Chanukah light, the Gemara, the siddur and Tehillim until Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens the meal of Zos Chanukah by explaining that because Chanukah was established for praise and thanksgiving, singing praises makes its meal a seudas mitzvah. He then asks why the Chashmonaim, who were holy, took kingship, and answers that, like Moshe Rabbeinu, they rose through extraordinary mesirus nefesh to the 'eighth world' above measure, where one person can be both king and kohen. He shows the same idea in the Masorah's counting of words in Mikeitz. Through the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel and the two orders of the tribes, he explains why for Beis Hillel the last day, falling in Teves, is the main day. Zos Chanukah is a later sealing after Yom Kippur, for later generations who did not finish their teshuvah. For Beis Hillel the main day of Chanukah is the last, when eight lights are lit, and it falls in Teves; for Beis Shammai it is the first day, in Kislev.
Zos Chanukah is a later time of sealing, after Yom Kippur and Hoshana Rabbah, for Jews who did teshuvah but did not complete it.
On Zos Chanukah the Shechina descends to the lowly Jews who stayed outside, and judges each by his hidden or haganuz rather than by his outward deeds.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yosef stood above the Shevatim as one of the seven 'shepherds', that his sphere was taharah, and that his purity gave the grain he sold in Egypt a taste and smell of kedushah, from which Yaakov knew he was alive.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Shovavim, the six weeks after Sefer Bereishis ends with Yosef's passing, as the time to draw down Yosef's kedushah. He asks why Yaakov loved Yosef for teaching him the Torah of Shem and Ever, and why Yaakov needed a teacher when Avraham grasped the whole Torah alone. He answers with the seven 'shepherds' (the ushpizin), each tied to a day, a middah and a seder of Mishnah: Avraham, the first, includes all, so he needed no teacher; each other shepherd grasped his own seder. Yosef, sixth, is Taharos, so Yaakov taught him only five sedarim, which showed he stood above the Shevatim. Through 'the power of the maker is in the made', Yosef's taharah gave the grain he sold a good taste and smell, from which Yaakov sensed he lived. The Rav turns to today's severe trials, calls for purity, Torah and tefillah, and closes with Hashem's love for those who withstand them.

en: Shovavim follows the end of Sefer Bereishis with Yosef's passing, and its six weeks are meant to draw down Yosef's kedushah of taharah.
Each of the seven shepherds corresponds to a day of the week, a middah and a seder of Mishnah, and grasped his own seder of the Torah without a teacher.
Avraham, the first of the shepherds, includes all of them, which is why he grasped the entire Torah himself and needed no teacher.
Yosef is a shepherd and not one of the Shevatim; his seder is Taharos, so Yaakov had to teach him only five sedarim, and this is why he loved him most.
Because the power of the maker enters what he makes, Yosef's purity put a good taste and smell into the grain he sold, and Yaakov sensed from it that Yosef was alive.
The Rav says today's world is one great Mitzrayim with unprecedented trials, and a Jew must know he is Hashem's emissary to stand firm in it.

He sets out the three levels of Avos, seven shepherds and Shevatim, each shepherd giving all of Klal Yisrael a path in serving Hashem, and shows from Rashi on 'even Yisrael' that Yosef, a son with the level of a father, stood above the Shevatim.

title.en: Days, middos and the sedarim of Mishnah

summary.en: The Rav explains the order of Chok LeYisrael, which ties each day of the week to a middah and a seder of Mishnah and Gemara. From this he concludes that each shepherd, aligned with one seder, grasped that seder himself without a teacher, as all will in the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Avraham includes all; Yosef is Taharos

summary.en: From the Zohar on the ushpizin and the rule that a first letter includes the whole word, the Rav explains that Avraham, the first shepherd, includes all seven and so needed no teacher, while Yaakov had to receive the other sedarim. Yosef, the sixth, is Taharos, so Yaakov taught him only five sedarim; this explains the Baal HaTurim and why Yaakov loved him above his brothers.

title.en: Emunah, taharah and the taste of fruit

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the six sedarim are hinted in a passuk beginning with 'emunah', and says Avraham's emunah includes the whole Torah. He then explains that taharah, Yosef's quality and the preparation for Shabbos, was a great level in Bayis times, and that since taharah ceased the taste and smell of fruit departed.

title.en: Why Yosef himself sold the grain

summary.en: The Rav asks why the ruler of Egypt personally sold grain, like a president working in a fruit store. Beyond the simple answer that he wanted to meet his brothers, he explains through 'the power of the maker is in the made' that Yosef's taharah entered the grain, and that Yaakov, tasting and smelling kedushah in it, knew Yosef was alive, which ties Rashi's two readings together.

title.en: The Yishmaelim's spices and Yosef's fragrance

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Arabia took most of the world's immorality and Rashi's chiddush that the Yishmaelim who carried Yosef bore fragrant spices instead of foul-smelling goods. Following Rav Tzadok, he explains that nations clothe a bad trait in an outer show, but Yosef's taharah brought a good smell, and he brings the Gemara that bachurim who never tasted sin will give off a fragrance like Levanon. He concludes that Shovavim is for taking taharah from Yosef.

title.en: Shovavim of old; purity and the taste of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav recalls the Satmar Rav speaking during Shovavim in Williamsburg over sixty years ago, with the beis medrash packed and no dry eye. He says that in our situation every young man must know this time is set aside for taharah, and that only one who is pure can feel kedushah and taste in Shabbos, tefillah and Torah, in contrast to bachurim who complain that Shabbos bores them.

title.en: Today's trials and our mission

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the moral world of earlier years with today's open street and the new devices that bring the yetzer hara into Jewish homes. He says these are the trials of ikvesa d'Meshicha described at the end of Sotah, that Hashem sends no trial one cannot pass, and that in this world, one great Mitzrayim, a Jew is Hashem's emissary to stay strong in Torah, tefillah and kedushah.

title.en: Precious to Hashem: 'Yaakov, Yaakov'

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Chaim Vital's account that the Arizal told him a person of this late generation is very great, and says every act of holding back is precious to Hashem. From 'Yaakov, Yaakov', a term of love said as Yaakov went down to Egypt, he says Hashem loves the bachur who keeps himself pure there; Sefer Bereishis ends with Yosef's passing, one must strengthen oneself, and the tikkun is immersing in learning. He closes with a brachah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: ר”ה שחל בשבת - Developing a Relationship with our Advocate

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos and the shofar is silent, Shabbos itself becomes the advocate of the Jewish people, so before the Day of Judgment one must make peace with Shabbos and learn to keep it properly.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a parable, adapted from a sefer's Rosh Hashanah drasha for a year when Rosh Hashanah fell on Shabbos: a king's faithful servant dies, and his son is sent to mine gems for the king but neglects his task. Each year the finance minister pleads for him, but one year the minister is absent and the princess, whom the son had abused, takes his place; a wise man tells him to beg her forgiveness, and she pleads his case. The Rav explains: the king is Hashem, the gems are Torah and mitzvos, the regular advocate is the shofar, and when Rosh Hashanah is on Shabbos, Shabbos, the king's daughter and our cousin, pleads instead. Since we have wronged Shabbos, we must make up with her: learn hilchos Shabbos, refine Shabbos speech, and fill Shabbos with kedushah and joy, illustrated by two stories of tzaddikim. He closes urging a new kabbalah in the area of Shabbos for this year.

en: In an ordinary year the shofar is the advocate that pleads for Klal Yisrael on Rosh Hashanah, carrying their teshuvah before Hashem.

When Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos and the shofar is not blown, Shabbos itself takes over as the advocate, and since Shabbos is the King's daughter and bound up with the Jewish soul, an even better year can be expected.
Because Jews have wronged Shabbos through chillul Shabbos, they must make peace with Shabbos through teshuvah before Rosh Hashanah, so that she pleads for them rather than against them.
One cannot keep Shabbos properly without knowing hilchos Shabbos, which are numerous and complex, so the Rav calls for learning them until one masters them.

Keeping Shabbos means more than avoiding its prohibitions: it is a day of rest and kedushah, with refined speech and a way of spending it that gives pleasure to Shabbos, which then gives pleasure back.
For a Jew who keeps it properly, Shabbos is the most joyous day of the week, a pleasure no worldly delight can match.

title.en: Parable of the king, the gems and the princess

summary.en: The Rav tells a parable of a faithful servant's son sent to mine gems for the king, who neglects his work and is saved each year by the finance minister, until one year the princess he had abused must judge him and a wise man tells him to beg her forgiveness. He says he adapted it from a sefer's drasha for a Rosh Hashanah that fell on Shabbos.

title.en: The nimshal: the shofar as our advocate

summary.en: The Rav explains the parable: the king is Hashem, the beloved servant is the Avos, the gems are Torah and mitzvos the Jews must produce in this world, and the friendly minister is the shofar, whose every sound is a plea for forgiveness accompanied by the teshuvah of the Jewish heart.

title.en: When Rosh Hashanah is Shabbos, Shabbos pleads

summary.en: When Rosh Hashanah is on Shabbos and the shofar is not blown, Shabbos, the King's daughter and the Jew's cousin through the neshamah yeseirah, takes over the case; the Rav brings the seforim's reading of 'Tiku bachodesh shofar' whose initials spell Shabbos. But since Jews have abused Shabbos, the Torah, the wise man of the court, tells them to do teshuvah, beg Shabbos's forgiveness and promise to keep her.

title.en: Making peace with Shabbos: learning its halachos

summary.en: Since Shabbos rather than the shofar will plead this Rosh Hashanah, the Rav says one must first be on good terms with Shabbos. He challenges the assumption that one keeps Shabbos already: without knowing the many complex halachos, such as the thirty-nine melachos, borer and muktzeh, one surely stumbles, so one should resolve to learn hilchos Shabbos thoroughly.

title.en: Beyond the prohibitions: holy speech and rest

summary.en: The Rav explains that avoiding issurim is not enough: Shabbos is a day of rest and kedushah. Since Hashem created the world in six days through speech, one rests on Shabbos by refining one's speech; Shabbos is not for sleeping and reading the newspaper but for kedushah and tefillah, and when a Jew gives Shabbos pleasure, Shabbos reciprocates.

title.en: The poritz's summer sled and Nishmas

summary.en: The Rav tells of a poritz who spread sugar on a meadow to go sled riding in August; a chassid told his Rebbe how the poritz enjoys the world, and the Rebbe answered that it could not compare to his pleasure saying Nishmas on Shabbos morning. He contrasts people who complain Shabbos is boring with a Jew who keeps Shabbos and is repaid with a pleasure beyond anything worldly.

title.en: Reb Moshe Leib Sassover at the poritz's feast

summary.en: The Rav tells of Reb Moshe Leib Sassover, who went to the paritzim to redeem Jews imprisoned for unpaid rent; at a poritz's feast on a fast day, the aroma of a costly dish endangered him, and he saved himself by recalling his pleasure saying Nishmas on Shabbos. The Rav concludes that Shabbos is the most joyous day, but only for one who keeps it as it should be kept.

title.en: A new kabbalah for Shabbos this year

summary.en: The Rav urges keeping Shabbos as the day of Hashem's joy in His creation, and brings from seforim that on Rosh Hashanah each person should take on a new hanhagah; he suggests it be in the area of Shabbos, so that one can say 'Retzei vimnuchaseinu' to Hashem. He notes that this year Shabbos reigns, with Rosh Hashanah, Sukkos and two Shabbosos of Chanukah, and closes with a brachah for the eternal Shabbos.

catalogTitle: ישראל נקראים על שם השבעה פירות שנשתבחו בהן א"י (שייכות לפרשת ליתרו)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the seven species are ranked by their closeness to the word 'Eretz', which alludes to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim, and that every Jew, even the lowest, is one of these fruits and is bound to Eretz like the pomegranate.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shir Hashirim's 'your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates', which Rashi applies to the smallest Jews, and with the year's division into four quarters, where Teves and Shevat, like Tammuz and Av, belong to the low last quarter until Tu B'Shvat. He brings the Midrash that the spies were told to take pomegranates and the Gemara in Berachos that the order of blessings follows closeness to the word 'Eretz'. Eretz, he explains, alludes to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim, which is why Moshe repeats it in Devarim. The pomegranate is farthest from Eretz, yet still bound to it. He applies this to Acher and Rabbi Meir, to the dispute of Rav Hamnuna and Rav Chisda, to hair covering and Kimchis, and to the duty to raise up the distant. He closes that every Jew is one of the fruits, and with tefillos for Tu B'Shvat.

en: The importance of each of the seven species follows how close it stands to the word 'Eretz' in the passuk, since Eretz alludes to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim.
Eretz Yisrael corresponds to Olam Haba, so going there, supporting it, eating its fruits and even speaking of it awaken yiras shamayim; for this Moshe repeats the word Eretz throughout Devarim.
The pomegranate is the farthest of the species from Eretz, yet it is still bound to it; so too the lowest Jews, and the low months of the year, remain bound to yiras shamayim.
Teves and Shevat, like Tammuz and Av, are the last and lowest quarter of the year, but from the fifteenth of the month the second half is already taken back into holiness.
Every Jew can identify with one of the seven fruits, and the Torah teaches that the distant one, the pomegranate, must be brought closer and raised up.

candidateTopics: months of the year and their quarters

title.en: Shabbos, Matan Torah and an orchard of pomegranates

summary.en: After brief opening words linking the week's reading of Matan Torah to Shabbos, the Rav brings the passuk 'your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates'. With Rashi he reads it as a dry field that must be watered, and as the smallest Jews, who are full of good deeds like a pomegranate.

title.en: The four quarters of the year and its last part

summary.en: The Rav explains that the year, like the twelve tribes in their four camps and the letters of the Torah, divides into four parts, the last being like the camp of Dan. Whether one counts from Tishrei or Nissan, Tammuz-Av or Teves-Shevat form the low last quarter, yet Elul and Adar, and the second halves of Av and Shevat, are taken back into holiness. He links the last letters of the Torah to the last generations before Moshiach.

title.en: 'Take of the fruit of the land': the pomegranates

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Moshe told the spies to take pomegranates, notes that 'ha'aretz' and 'rimon' share a gematria, and stresses that a gematria must fit the inner content of the matter. He then brings the Gemara in Berachos that the order of blessings follows the species' closeness to the word 'Eretz', so dates come before pomegranates, and asks what lies in that word.

title.en: Eretz alludes to Olam Haba

summary.en: Asking why the word Eretz appears in almost every chapter of Devarim, the Rav explains that Eretz alludes to Olam Haba, as the Mishnah reads 'they will inherit the land', and that Eretz Yisrael below corresponds to it. Therefore going to Eretz Yisrael, supporting it, eating its fruits and even speaking of it bring yiras shamayim, and Moshe repeated the word to awaken it.

title.en: The name Yisrael and the ranking of the fruits

summary.en: The Rav adds that speaking of tzaddikim also brings yiras shamayim, and reads 'Shema Yisrael... a land flowing with milk and honey' as Moshe's wish that the very name of a Jew should arouse it like the name Eretz. The seven species draw from Eretz Yisrael, so each one's rank follows its closeness to the word Eretz: the pomegranate, fifth after the first Eretz, is the farthest.

title.en: The shiurim learned from the seven species

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the whole passuk of the seven species was said for measures of halacha, and goes through them. Each species gives a positive measure the Torah speaks of, except the pomegranate, which marks the point at which a vessel is no longer a vessel; it speaks of what lies outside the Torah's measures.

title.en: The spies in the low months, and Moshe's advice

summary.en: The Rav explains that the spies went in Tammuz and Av, the pomegranate of the year, felt a fall and lost their desire for Torah and avodah, while the Chiddushei HaRim teaches one must serve Hashem in light and in darkness. Moshe's instruction to take pomegranates was strength for such a time: even the farthest is bound to Eretz, and by binding oneself to yiras shamayim, ehrliche Yidden and Olam Haba one passes through hard times.

title.en: Acher, Rabbi Meir: date or pomegranate

summary.en: Returning to 'your shoots', the Rav says the lowest Jews are like pomegranates. He brings the Gemara in Chagigah: Rabbi Meir learned from Acher, explained as eating a date and throwing away the pit, yet Heaven did not quote him; when Rabbah bar Shila compared it to a pomegranate, eating the inside and throwing away the peel, it was accepted. The Rav asks why, and gives a first answer: a date's waste is inside, a pomegranate's is outside.

title.en: Rav Hamnuna and Rav Chisda: what 'Eretz' means

summary.en: The Rav offers his own answer through the Gemara in Berachos: Rav Hamnuna blessed on dates before pomegranates, saying the date is second to Eretz and the pomegranate fifth. He explains the dispute by the difference between 'a cup of wine' and 'a cup of gold': for Rav Chisda Eretz is only the place where the fruit grows, so the order of the passuk decides; for Rav Hamnuna the fruits are bound to the essence of Eretz, so closeness to the word decides.

title.en: Why Rabbah bar Shila's answer was accepted

summary.en: The Rav applies the dispute: if Acher is hinted in a fruit at all, it is the last one. By the view that the last is the date, which has no bond to Eretz, Torah learned from Acher has no bond to Olam Haba and Heaven did not say it; Rabbah bar Shila held that the last is the pomegranate, bound to Eretz, so even Rabbi Meir's Torah from Acher comes from Olam Haba and was accepted. He connects this to 'even the empty ones among you are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate'.

title.en: Hair covering, the pomegranate and Kimchis

summary.en: The Rav discusses the Rashba's view, brought in the Shulchan Aruch's commentaries, about hair that slips out of the braid, against the Zohar's demand to cover every hair. Such hair is like the pomegranate, last yet bound to Eretz; women who cover all their hair are like the date; and Kimchis, whose walls never saw her hair, is like wheat, first after the first Eretz. He asks why the Gemara mentions that she was a seller of flour.

title.en: Why Eretz twice, and raising up the pomegranate

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah writes Eretz twice rather than listing the fruits in order. He answers that writing it once would let one think Eretz is only a vessel for the fruits; writing it twice shows that all the fruits, and so all Jews, are bound to Eretz and Olam Haba. The Torah also places the pomegranate before the date and honey, to teach that the distant one must be brought close and lifted up, as the word 'rimon' suggests.

title.en: Every Jew is one of the fruits; Tu B'Shvat

summary.en: The Rav shows that Jews are compared to each of the seven species and that every Jew belongs to one of them. On Tu B'Shvat, when one makes a blessing over fruits as the Magen Avraham brings, Hashem as it were makes a blessing over the Jews and rejoices with them; he speaks of the golden fruits Shlomo planted in the Beis Hamikdash, and closes with tefillos for a fine esrog and for good, golden fruits.
